utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. A few matters. Mr. Harmon -- and perhaps, Madam Usher, you could already try to find the witness so that he could be standby. Were you able to reduce the number of pages of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was, Your Honour. I informed the Defence last night in respect of tab 59, the pages that are relevant are pages 1 through 6 and pages 8 through 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. But I reserve the right again to challenge the admission of the exhibit when that becomes an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the presence of the witness is not of any relevance for that later objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we know that you reserve that right and we have now reduced the number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's on the record. Then, Mr. Josse, I think you provided the representative of the Registry with the CD concerning the attack on the Tuzla convoy, but I also do understand that there is no transcript, neither in English nor in B/C/S. Mr. Harmon, do you know whether that exists?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please try to find out. Because I don't know whether there is any text spoken on it or whether it's just pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was on -- it was being played by a member of our team when I left this courtroom last night, and I viewed a small portion of it and there is some text -- there is spoken words. I wasn't exactly clear even by asking him what they were. He's in this building. I can try and find out. The trouble, of course, is, from our point of view, preparing a text would be a mammoth task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how much text there is. If it's just a journalist who says this is a convoy that leaves Tuzla and it's now attacked by the Green Berets or whatever, then of course the parties could even agree that the text is, for our understanding, not of major importance but it's just the event that is described.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what I was rather assuming, but permit me to deal with it this morning. I'd like to deal, whilst it's fresh in our memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The person concerned is in the building, I repeat, and I'll speak to him at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else at this moment? I do understand that you have replaced number 60; is that right? Tab 60, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's tab 60, yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Poplasen into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poplasen. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Harmon will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all let me start with the two documents that I gave you copies of last night. You asserted they were forgeries. Have you had an opportunity to look at those documents and can you enlighten us as to any particular features of those documents that suggest they are forgeries? Starting with the document that is found in tab 37, if you would, Mr. Poplasen. That is the Serbian Democratic Party decision of 9 September 1991, on your appointment to the Commission for Information and Propaganda.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've reviewed both documents. As for the first one, I didn't say it was a forgery. I simply said that I saw it for the first time yesterday. I'm not saying that this isn't authentic but I found out that I was appointed to this commission for the first time yesterday. As far as the second document is concerned, my assessment of it being a forgery has to do only with the fact that my name was listed among those attending the meeting of the commission. I have absolutely no recollection of either being a member of the commission or ever attending any of its meetings. Who wrote this document, I do not know, but I'm not saying that it -- this document isn't an authentic one. I don't know. I really cannot comment on its contents and I don't recall attending a meeting or ever being on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Poplasen. Let me turn my attention now to a slightly different topic. I'm interested in your defining a term that I have seen frequently used by you and representatives of your party and representatives of the SDS. That is the term "genocide." And in the context of the discussions that -- in which you participated, there was frequent reference to a fear of genocide reoccurring in Bosnia. I'm not interested in the historical context of that. What I'm interested in is when that -- when you used that term, what did you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it in the shortest of terms, by "genocide" I mean an organised, deliberate, planned, physical, cultural and spiritual extermination of a group. Most often the group is consisted of members of a nation. Extermination can be of different characters, in terms of a pogrom, of an extermination of a religious group, or it can be a cultural genocide, when the culture of a peoples is considered to be inappropriate and one aims or strives to destroy any elements underlying the culture of a peoples. But what is most significant and most important, at least as far as the events on the Balkans are concerned, is the organised, planned and deliberate designed destruction of a peoples, behind which a state is hiding or a political or any other organisation sponsored or supported by a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Let me turn to your work as a republican commissioner. You told us earlier that you worked closely with Mr. Koljevic in your capacity as a war commissioner. You informed Mr. Koljevic, as you were required to do. Mr. Koljevic's responsibility was to inform the other leaders in the Republika Srpska; Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mrs. Plavsic, of the work of the commissioners and what information they were giving to him. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, and he did that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he did. I suppose he submitted a sort of a rough report to the other members of the Presidency. He probably did not go into detail. There were several commissioners, and if each one of them presented Mr. Koljevic with a detailed report, then it would have been quite a difficult task for Professor Koljevic to relay the information in full. Probably he made a summary of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you left and you delegated your authority as a republican commissioner to a number of individuals. Did they continue to inform Mr. Koljevic of events in the municipality where you served as a republican commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that the municipality of Vogosca, being a municipality belonging to Sarajevo, was not too far from the seat of the Presidency and the government of Republika Srpska, so that in performing their duties, they were able to relay the information directly to Professor Koljevic. Particularly because I was often away in other parts of the republic and in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in fact, they signed documents on your behalf. I'm going to be presenting you with some of those documents later this morning. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review the documents that were signed on your behalf at a later time, post facto?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They informed me verbally of having submitted their reports, and in principle I did not require them to do so, especially as far as the functioning of the local authorities was concerned, but if there was a report submitted to the Presidency and the government, I wanted to be privy to that, because we saw some of the documents that we commented on, where we said that the Presidency -- or that the commissioners worked in cooperation with the local authorities, and if there were any decisions made which in a way derogated from the authorities of the competent organs, then this constituted a violation of the regulations. And there were such instances, in fact, although the violations were not so grave, and I thought that the Executive Board of the Vogosca Municipal Assembly did in fact perform its duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned yesterday, Mr. Poplasen, a gentleman by the name of Mr. Radovanovic. You were asked specifically about him by Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to page 42 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said he was a republican commissioner for the municipality of Ilidza and you were critical of him. You said he left most of his duties and obligations to the president of the Ilidza municipality, and that also included the reporting obligations. Let me ask you: Mr. Radovanovic was also the commissioner for the Serb municipality of Rajlovac, which was nearby, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that Rajlovac had the status of a municipality. Rajlovac is a settlement. There was the municipality of Vogosca and the neighbouring municipality was that of Ilidza. It is possible that at a later stage this area in fact became a municipality, but as far as I know, in 1992, while we were working as commissioners, Rajlovac was not a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to present you with a document in just a moment that will show you there was a self-declared municipality of Rajlovac, but let me ask you: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Jovo Bozic who was the president of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Radovanovic had responsibilities as a war commissioner for more than the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. Mr. Radovanovic should know that. If that is the case, there should be a document in relation to this. Such a duty cannot be delegated verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 38 needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 38, Your Honours, will be P1086.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, tab 38 is the wrong exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We need to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 38 was assigned a number yesterday already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll return to it, Your Honour. I'll return to it at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we'll come back to that document, Mr. Poplasen. I'll show you after the break, rather than take time now. Let me turn to the relationship between the SDS and the -- and your party, the Serb Radical Party, and the cooperation that existed in 1992. If we can turn to tab 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And tab 14 needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1087, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, tab 14 is a document from February issue, issue number 12 of a publication entitled "Velika Serbia." It is entitled: "Visit by Vojislav Seselj to Serbian volunteer units in Banja Luka." It's author is Nikodin Cavic, president of the Serbian Radical Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'd like to direct your attention, if I can, to a passage in this document. It is found in the B/C/S version, I believe, on page 21 of the document, between -- midway between the second and the third photographs, so it should be to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the passage I'm referring to is on page 3 in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- I'm quoting Dr. Seselj. This is what the passage says,

utterances.speaker: MR. POPLASEN
utterances.text: "Dr. Vojislav Seselj said that the Serbian Radical Party shall in no way whatsoever stand in the way of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina but quite the reverse. It will be its good associate. Support, encouragement and all the things which are of vital interest to the survival of the Serbian people in these lands will be done through joint effort and understanding." Now, that was -- that's a fair characterisation of how the SRS and the SDS worked in 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to see, this dates from 1991. The text and the qualification. You yourself said that the text was from 1992. Although I can't find it here, I should see which issue this is of the magazine of Velika Serbia, although I can't see. All right, it is here at the end; Banja Luka, 27 December, 1991. Therefore, this isn't 1992, this is 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. I was informed it was 1992. You're correct. I see that date at the bottom. But getting to the point I would like you to comment on, the passage that I read fairly reflects the way in which the SDS and the SRS worked in 1992. It was a cooperative relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. The date under an article, Mr. Poplasen, is not necessarily the same as the date of the publication. So whether Mr. Poplasen is correct, at least it seems that the author has dated this article late 1991 but when it was published is still unclear. So I just want to avoid any misunderstanding as that the Chamber would accept what seems to be agreed between Prosecution and witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are told, apparently, the date of publication in English in a handwritten entry on the top of page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that, but that's -- finds no source in the original so it should not have been there, as a matter of fact, in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's why I raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon is invited to see whether the original, with the date, could be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even agreement between the parties would be enough for me. We don't have to see it. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me return to the question I've been asking you, Mr. Poplasen. The passage that I read to you fairly characterises the manner in which the Serb Radical Party - your party in Bosnia - and the SDS party worked in 1992; it was a cooperative relationship. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. But I can help you understand the background, the whole context, in a few sentences, if I'm allowed. You see, at the time when this was authored, I was living and working in Sarajevo, in peace. These events related here have to do with the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina for the most part, and this information I was only able to glean from the papers. The quotation you cited here, well, I've explained on several occasions that we had quite a cooperative relationship with the SDS whenever it suited us. Evidently, the information contained in your question is true because this particular aspect was consistent with what our positions were, and I'm referring to what the SDS was doing in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the objectives that were sought to be achieved in Bosnia, were there differences in the policy between the SRS party in Bosnia and the SRS party in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think there were any. In essence, it was a united party. There were -- there was a joint platform, joint documents. There was this central body called the Central Homeland Administration. I explained to you that the Serbian Radical Party of the Republic of Srpska was formally independent because Bosnia-Herzegovina had been internationally recognised, in view of the fact that the party wanted to take part in the elections and it had to be registered as a political party in the country where it wanted to participate in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, Mr. Poplasen, to tab 59, then. I want to ask you about a portion of the text in tab 59.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak closer to the microphone or maybe switch another microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I'd like to direct your attention to page 188 in the Cyrillic text, and Your Honours' attention to the bottom of page 8 and the top of -- I'm sorry, bottom of page 10, Your Honour, going over to the next page. Now, let me read this portion of the text to you, Mr. Poplasen. This is in the context of a discussion about forming a new state. The question that is asked is: "A treatment of non-Serbs in the process of unification is a particular issue. Who is forming the state, what kind of state and in which borders?" Quotation: "This is inevitable formation of a civilian state, the state of the Serbs and equal (loyalty is implicit) citizens, members of other nations, ethnic minorities and groups. "If such a state is formed, other nations, ethnic minorities and groups should not exceed more than 8 per cent of total population; they should not exceed the said percentage in any larger settlement, region or administrative unit, and there should be no possibility to change that percentage through birth rate. That is an important reason to determine the borders by respecting this German standard. "Therefore, the State would have to be peaceful, democratic, with multi-party political system and market-oriented economy." Mr. Poplasen, did that discussion vis-a-vis ethnic minorities reflect the position of the SRS in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the reasoning by Mr. Seselj, which in my opinion should be changed in some details. I do not wish to elaborate on the percentage. It could be interpreted differently. It could mean that a -- doesn't have to be a strict measure concerning the birth rate or possible emigration. In my opinion, any mentioning of a percentage in relation to the population is quite unnecessary, but in any case I agree with the statement that the state would have to be peaceful, democratic, with multi-party political system and market oriented economy. But this in itself already excludes the other. The two are quite contradictory, and therefore in this view point of Mr. Seselj's there are some contradictions that a logic cannot accept, and this cannot reflect a serious stance by a political party. Doesn't reflect my position, at any rate. This is probably an ad hoc statement. He probably came across some German standards and at the time of the interview he felt it important historically to emphasise the importance of the preservation of the nation, but he should be the one to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But your attitude towards the Muslims, and the party, the SRS party's attitude towards Muslims in a newly created Serbian state or entity in Bosnia was that they should be in a minority. You didn't want to live with them, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We insisted on a common state with the Muslims, and we launched initiatives for such negotiations. Some of them called it a Yugoslavia in miniature, or a rump Yugoslavia. Yesterday, I was interrupted by the Presiding Judge when I wanted to explain what I meant by an inter-agreement. The presidents of the republics had already agreed on this before the war. They had not only agreed on it, they signed the Cutileiro Plan, and it meant coexistence. And then Alija Izetbegovic, under pressure of the American ambassador, withdrew his signature and war broke out. So it's not the case that the parties' position was to have an ethnically clean area and that the members of the other ethnicities were enemies and that we were in a conflict. Our approach was that of a common state because it was quite clear that Slovenia no longer wished to be part of Yugoslavia. The problem of Croatia arose, which had a large Croatian -- Serb population, and the idea was to form a joint state where all the Serbs, Muslims and Albanians would live together and regulate their relations. When the broker -- when the war broke out, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the war broke out, you didn't want to live with the Muslims, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How was one to live in such a state when you would get killed? You could only live in it if you were in the graveyard. I was unable to enter Sarajevo although I didn't do anything. And 10 days later I was declared a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, is it a fact that you considered the Muslim nation a fictional nation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they considered, and they no longer called themselves Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you consider the Muslims a fictional nation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because this is a religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for a clarification of one of your last answers, Mr. Poplasen. You said before the war, you negotiated to live together with the other nationalities or ethnicities, whatever you call it; with the Muslims. Then you said, after the war broke out, "How was one to live in such a state when you would get killed?" Do I understand that to be that you did not want to live together with Muslims and Croats in a united Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a distinction was made here between the time preceding the war and the period when the war broke out. In the pre-war period, I explained that there were efforts to preserve a joint state, because I was part of it. I lived there, just as other people did. However, when the war broke out, the relations changed, the motives changed. That there were efforts at preserving Yugoslavia is shown not only by the Cutileiro Plan but a series of talks with the representatives of the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear to me. You explained that and I understand that fully. But then you said, when you were asked about once the war had broken out, that -- how could you live with them in a state? The only thing I asked you is what state you were referring to. Were you referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state in which you could not live with those who threatened your life? Is that how I should understand "a state"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evidently, there is a bit of a misunderstanding here. When the war started, it was impossible to enter Sarajevo, physically speaking, because there were fortified positions on both sides. Some 15 to 20 days later - I don't recall this precisely - I read it in a paper, the faculty of political science dismissed me, and although it was not within the faculty's competence, the faculty declared me a war criminal. And now the Prosecutor asked me whether I would have lived with the Muslims under those circumstances. It is a question that cannot be answered. How can I live there if I'm dismissed from my job, I'm declared a war criminal, I'm not allowed entry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand your answer to be, "How could I live with the Muslims in a state, being Bosnia-Herzegovina, where they made life impossible for me?" Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the territory of the federation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I move one step forward. Now, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or later Republika Srpska, has been created. That means that you more or less separated from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were not claimed by or were not dominated by Serbs. Now, my question now is, how about living together on Republika Srpska territory, or Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the earlier stages? Would you consider that in municipalities within Republika Srpska territory, let's just assume 40 per cent Serbs, 30 per cent Muslims, would you live with the Muslims in those areas together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I did. There were Muslims, and there still are in Banja Luka and elsewhere, both during the war and now. There was no obstacle to that, no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From the figures this Chamber has received, there still are Muslims, although their number has been drastically reduced. So therefore I'm asking not whether you're living at this moment with small numbers of Muslims, and it differs from one municipality to another, but at that time, did you consider it feasible to live, well let's say in a municipality with a 40 per cent Serbs and the 30 per cent Muslims remaining in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The principle is clear: Of course, it would have been feasible back then, but I don't really want to go into percentages. The percentages depend on the situation. Yes, it would have been feasible back then and it did happen, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if there was a Muslim majority in one of the municipalities claimed by the Republika Srpska, would you think it feasible and would you support - because that was not in my last question - would you support living together even if a Muslim majority might get a majority in municipal organs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with the proviso that the laws and the regulations of the Republika Srpska are complied with. That was the only condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did that, in your experience, happen anywhere on Republika Srpska territory? Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have such an experience. You're quite right in saying that there was a huge decrease in the percentage of the Muslim population in most municipalities within the framework of the Republika Srpska, but at the same time the opposite is true as well. I mean, in most municipalities on the territory of the federation, the Serbs have almost disappeared. So it's a general phenomenon in the BH. There were huge movements of population, and people were trying to avoid situations in which they felt threatened and insecure, so it is not only typical of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not saying that it was typical for Republika Srpska. What did make Serbs move out of the federation territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of thousands of testimonies, there was a general sense of being unsafe and insecure. In Sarajevo, for example, several thousands of Serbs -- I mean, quite a few of them were killed, and many people were automatically laid off within just a couple of days. Many were gotten rid of in order for other people to get their hands on their property, on their real estate, et cetera. And there was a general atmosphere in which it was sufficient for a person to be a member of the Serb nation in order to be totally threatened. Even their lives were at risk. And for example, there were these changes in percentages on the territory of Sarajevo, and that was the case elsewhere throughout the federation as well, in other municipalities. There are documents that do exist. There are about 4.000 missing Serbs in Sarajevo and nobody knows what happened to them. And the Ministry of the Interior is in the possession of these documents, as well as the Association of Camp Inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this organised and/or tolerated by the federation authorities or organs? So this behaviour against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in the federation myself, but according to secondhand evidence from my point of view, obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you -- I asked you what caused the Serbs to leave federation territory. Could you tell us what caused the Muslims to leave Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably they would be better placed to reply to that question, but I think that there must have been such situations in the Republika Srpska as well, in reverse. Everybody was losing their jobs and there was a general feeling of mistrust. There were some exaggerated situations, some abuse, mistreatment, probably murders - I'm not arguing against that - and I think these cases were dealt with in different ways. So there is a whole range of reasons. Probably they felt safer in an area in which the Muslims were in majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, for the reasons why Serbs were leaving, you said: "... quite a few of them were killed, many people were automatically laid off within a couple of days. Many were gotten rid of in order for other people to get their hands on their property, on their real estate, et cetera. And there was a general atmosphere in which it was sufficient for a person to be a member of the Serb nation in order to be totally threatened. Even their lives were at risk." Would this be -- this description would be true for the other situation as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me, and you're using the conditional. Yes, it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you talked about 4.000 Serbs missing in Sarajevo, would you consider that a similar thing may have happened on the other side? That means large numbers of Muslims or Croats missing on Republika Srpska territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose it is, indeed, possible. I've just told you, yes, it could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this general atmosphere of threats and fear, was that -- on the Republika Srpska side, was that, as I asked for the other situation, was that tolerated by the Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that respect, we've heard a number of conversations. As far as I know, the authorities insisted in documents, in some kinds of guidelines, directives, and so on and so forth, on the need for free movement and the respect of all international conventions and regulations pertaining to human rights issues, the kind of behaviour with respect to the POWs, and I think to the extent to which it was possible, it was being prevented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say -- but thank you for your answers. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me go to the next exhibit, Your Honours. This is Extra 3 defined on the list. It needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1088, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, we are going to play a portion of a tape. This tape, Mr. Poplasen, is from a TV broadcast relating to the post-Dayton elections. It occurred on the 6th of August. The participants were Zlatko Lagundzija of the SDP party; Rasema Magazinovic of the BH Women's Party; yourself; Petar Jovic, BH Citizens' Democratic Party; Dubravka Lovrenovic of the Croatian Peasant Party; Dragomir Grubac of the Patriotic Bloc; Simo Simic of the Union of BH Socio-democrats; Dragutin Ilic of the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska; and Miodrag Zivanovic of the RS Socio-liberal Party. We are going to play part of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it needs a number, Mr. Registrar. Extra 3, and you said 6th of August but I take it that it was 6th of August 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it has already 1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the transcript portion that will be played will start at the top of page 2 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we could play this, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Has the Dayton Agreement solved the Serbian national issue? "Just a moment ... I just wanted to ... "Please, go ahead ... "We are really facing the situation when there, over the Drina, when we have to fight for ... When I'm directly asked, I would really ... This is not the former Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "It seems like it is mine, sorry ... please. "Let it be there! You see, this is the first time I hear that one political document like the Dayton Agreement can be theoretical thesis for discussion on one question as Mr. ... says ... Now, listen, it is theoretical prefix for discussion, a political document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to be a problem. Mr. Poplasen, what's the problem? Can't you hear? Are you on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't hearing anything through my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps you could restart and see whether it now goes any better.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Did the Dayton Agreement solve the Serbian national issue? "Just a moment ... I just wanted to ... "Please, go ahead ... "We are really facing the situation when there, over the Drina, when we have to fight for ... When I'm directly asked, I would really ... This is not the former Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "It seems like it is mine, sorry ... please. "Let it be there! You see, this is the first time I hear that a political document like the Dayton Agreement can be a theoretical thesis for the discussion of one question as the gentleman here says ... Listen, now it is a theoretical prefix for discussion, a political document. Secondly, I tried to speak like television. Republika Srpska is a national issue. And now various new terminologies are being introduced. You know. When it comes to a national issue, it gets really complex. Those other ones who used to live with us have to tell me first if they are Bosnians, if they are Muslims or if they are Turks. This year they are Bosniaks, last year they were Muslims. Listen, it is a historical genesis. I'm not making it up. "Nikola, when you talked about those things before ... my friends Radil and Fadil thought that you were kidding. Now they saw that you're being serious. Don't be so serious ... Don't be, it is rude. "Well, we have to agree on it. "It is rude if you and I need to agree about such a thing. It is rude ... "There is a genesis ... A thesis was heard here that there were certain influences of other peoples, from outside and so on ... "... that anchors allow such conversation ... "And can I say what I think, Zlatko? "... Of course you can, Nikola. "Are you supposed to write a speech for me so that I read out what you and Alija came up with. "... No, you're the one who is used to writing speeches for others and reading them in the Marx Centre and not me, in which ... "... They could not even read ... "I would like to ask Mr. Lagundzija to wait until Mr. Poplasen finishes what he wants to say. I think it is -- "Zlatko still thinks that he is in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. Listen ... " ... reacts on these statements, not only did he react on first statement by Mrs. ... "Let Mr. Poplasen finish, please. "If one nation has been formed under the influence of external forces, as one of the gentlemen said, I now claim that the external forces have a critical influence on the political, military and economic events in the Balkans, and it is correct. So certain nations and quasi-nations were formed under certain influences. But that is not the subject of tonight's discussion. The subject is the Republika Srpska and a national issue. Please let me also support the cessation of bloodshed. Nobody can convince me that after four years of bloodshed when we all had, four years of war, we should again live together knowing that another bloodshed would take place. I'm convinced that the bloodshed will be stopped at the moment when we start visiting each other with passports. There is no reason ... There is no reason not to cooperate in all fields for which we estimate we have a joint interest. You see, four years of bloodshed, the whole world and everyone around ... judge the Serbs to be primitive and aggressive. They are guilty of everything. Now when we at the referendum twice vote in favour of the state independence, they are pushing us again. And we are no good and they still want to live with us. I simply cannot understand that. What it is all about? "And you don't want to live with us? "We don't want to. Of course we don't want to. "But why? "Because we don't want the bloodshed to be repeated. "Please, can you give me just example on the basis of which you can tell me that you don't wish to live with us?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last few lines were not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't see them either, Your Honour. We'll have to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's a reflection of your views in 1996 in respect of living with Muslims, isn't it, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but could I just say a few words before I answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me -- is that -- that was your attitude in 1996 at that time, in respect of living with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you first answer the question, then you may explain or give any further comment to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was my attitude in 1996 and it is still my attitude today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poplasen, you have tried to distinguish between your attitude before the war, during the war, and after the war. And this is your reflection of -- the video we've seen is a reflection of your attitude after the war. During the war, once the war started, it's also true, isn't it, that you and your party did not want to live, coexist, with Muslims on territory that had been historically claimed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before the war? What, I didn't quite understand what you said. What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During the war -- let me backtrack. There were territories that the Serbs considered historically their territory before the war and during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were their inheritance, their property. I don't know what you mean historically. They were theirs by right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read to you a sentence, then. Let me read a sentence to you in the same interview, Mr. Poplasen. We didn't play this part of the text, but I'll read it to you. It says -- at the first page of the transcript, it says: "I think it's necessary to point out and recall that the Serbs are one of the rare historical civilised European peoples who unfortunately and for various reasons in the last 200 years did not manage to define a national Serbian state in which a majority of Serbs would live together on the major part of the historical and ethnic territories populated by the Serbian people." That's what I'm referring to. There was a vision of what was historically Serbian territory. And that vision was one that you held before the war, held during the war, and held after the war. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a little bit more clear now. Yes. It is about centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Poplasen, on the -- during the war, you, your party, the SDS party, did not believe that the Muslims and the Serbs -- that Muslims and the Serbs could coexist together, did they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs wanted to achieve -- they had a certain vision and they wanted to achieve certain territories that historically had belonged to them. That was one of their objectives, one of your party's objectives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historically speaking is what I meant. It's private property. You just have to look at the land registers. If that's what you mean by "historically," yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, some of these territories that were claimed historically by the Serbs had majority Muslim population. For example, Zvornik statistically had 59 per cent Muslims, and the Serbs comprised 38 per cent of the population. Bratunac had 64 per cent of a Muslim population, the Serbs had 34 per cent. Brcko had 44 per cent Muslim, 25 per cent Croat, and 20 per cent Serb. How was it -- how were the Serbs going to achieve dominance in their -- in those historically -- those territories that were historically considered Serb?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably in a similar way as the other side managed to do it in Drvar where there was 98 per cent Serbs, in Petrovac 92 per cent, in another place 95 per cent, and they still don't belong to the Republika Srpska. So those events have to be seen in a broader context of military action, strategic directions, pressure brought to bear from the outside. At any rate, it is not a political concept that we are talking about, about a town in which the majority of the population is Muslim must be ethnically cleansed because it is a historically defined Serb city. That makes no sense at all. Zvornik could have a majority Muslim population and have an autonomous status, with all human rights being respected, and still be within the Republika Srpska. And the other way around: Had 98 per cent of Serbs been chased away from Drvar, they could have stayed there, but there are only very few of them left now. The mayor is elected there on the basis of 30 votes. You're putting a question to me which is about cosmic historical topics in order to show that I'm in favour of ethnic cleansing. I'm not in favour of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, Mr. Harmon put a question to you, that is how the Serbs were going to achieve dominance in those territories that were historically considered Serb, and he gave you three examples. Your answer was that presumably they would do it in a similar way as the other side managed to do it in -- and then you mentioned Drvar where 98 per cent were there, and you gave another example. How did they do it, the others, over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's not my answer. My answer consists of the following: Mr. Harmon's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I am reading the first part of your answer and I'm seeking clarification. You said presumably in a similar way as the other side managed to do it. How did the other side do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole thing consists of the following: Mr. Harmon's question contains a ready-made answer. He says, you wanted to dictate this; yes or no. It's not correct. If I were to ask him now to give me a yes or no answer -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, this is not the debating club. This is a court of law in which you're supposed to answer questions. You said Serbs were -- let me take the text. You said presumably in a similar way as the other side managed to do it. I want, because I do not know how you consider the other side managed to do it, so I'd like to seek clarification: How did the other side manage to do it, in your view, in the municipalities where there was a Serb majority? How did they do it? So I can understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By ethnic cleansing. The regular formations of the Croatian army, under the command of American generals, entered Bosnia and Herzegovina and for the most part chased away and to a considerable extent killed off big numbers of Serbs. There are TV documentaries about that, and commanders of the Croatian army and those American generals have wrote their memoirs -- have written their memoirs. So there are lots of dead, civilians, children, and so on. All those have been listed. And after those events, Serbs disappeared from those areas. So that was the action conducted in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is, when Mr. Harmon asked you how you would do that in Zvornik with 59 per cent Muslims, in Bratunac with 64 per cent Muslims, and Brcko with 44 per cent Muslims, the way - that's at least how I understand your answer - how the Serbs were going to achieve dominance was the same way as it was done in the other municipalities, and you just explained to us that the means used there -- well, to say it simply, was ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I supplemented my answer by saying that the question contained a ready-made answer, because the Prosecutor asked me in what way we wanted to achieve dictatorship, and to answer with a yes or no answer; whether it was done by pressure and military action, and so and so forth. My answer was that their goal was not to achieve dictatorship. And emotionally answering, I said the same way the other side did it because I did not want to answer a question which already contained a ready-made answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Harmon was talking about dominance and not about dictatorship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way it was interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps -- he was talking about dominance. But then in those municipalities with a majority of Muslims - Zvornik 59 per cent, Bratunac 64 per cent - they were claimed to be under the rule of Republika Srpska. How would you -- without using words dominance, without using words as dictatorship, how would you achieve to get these municipalities with a majority Muslims, how would you achieve to bring them under Republika Srpska rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the rule of law and equality. Equal human rights for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that was, you said, as long as they would obey to Republika Srpska rule. I mean, it was Republika Srpska who determined what was equality and what was equal human rights, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course. There are some universal principles which ought to be applied in the political policies and regulations of the Republika Srpska. There are some universal principles that cannot be circumvented, if we look at the European experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now looking back at those years, is it your opinion that Republika Srpska did provide this equal rights for all and the fundamental human rights to all living on the territory of Republika Srpska? Looking back to the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which period you have in mind. As far as the wartime period is concerned, it was a topic that could not be discussed. For as long as there are people getting killed, one cannot discuss these rights, and we have to defend the integrity of body and limb. As far as the post-war period is concerned, from 1996 onwards, I believe that major progress has been achieved in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly if I think you said that during the war, equal rights and fundamental freedoms could not be granted because one had to defend itself. And therefore, Republika Srpska could not grant it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evidently, neither of the sides could secure this. When there are large conflicts such as a war, which entails killing and many dead, one of the main mechanisms in the world in regulating these events is to achieve the separation of the warring parties. This is what the major powers have recourse to. In this TV show that we looked at a while ago, I insisted on this exact model in order to prevent any further bloodshed. Of course, separation can be provisional or permanent. I don't want to give you examples that we have experienced in the world because I wasn't asked that. After the first elections in 1996, it was -- or rather around the elections in 1996, it was my opinion that these nations ought to be separated in order to prevent war from occurring again, and then gradually work on bringing the peoples together, ensuring their cooperation and coexistence. But this is not something that can be ordered. Coexistence is not just a political category, it's also a moral and emotional category. I always found it difficult to understand how the world could make an assessment that the peoples in the -- in Yugoslavia could not coexist and that Yugoslavia ought to be dissolved, and then, on the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving away quite far from my question. Was separation of civilians necessary for those purposes as well, or would it be sufficient to get the armed forces under control and separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question. What do you mean the separation of civilians? Which civilians and which armed forces? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say that you can't live together any more once the war has started, and if you're living in municipalities not separated apart, perhaps, from village to village but mixed population, then to separate the peoples would need to move them, because they were a mixed population. Would it be necessary to separate by moving or by whatever other means you could suggest to me? Would it be necessary to separate the civilian population or would there have been a possibility to get control over armed forces so that new armed operations would be prevented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it's not the case of making a head count of each of the peoples and then separating them. Under the proviso that the Muslims and the Croats recognised the Republika Srpska, they are equal citizens, and vice versa. There is no problem there. As far as the separation is concerned, it applies not only to the state and territorial autonomy but also to personal autonomy, that members of a peoples can enjoy full human rights where they are a majority, and nobody would deny that they have their educational system and cultural rights. One has to presume that there is tolerance there. One has to also have the right to choose the school they wish to attend to. The separation does not only mean that you put someone on a bus and ship him off. This is -- the object should be the subject of careful negotiations and agreement, not necessarily entailing physical movement. Now, you should not have a political dictatorship where someone wants to leave and is not allowed to, where a person is dissatisfied with the situation and doesn't want to live in Sarajevo but wants to go to Banja Luka; or vice versa, if you have a person who doesn't want to live in Banja Luka and wishes to go to Sarajevo, and should be allowed to, just as the person who wants to stay where he is should be allowed to. As long as there are conditions in place that satisfy the person to the extent that he can fulfil himself in terms of culture, religion, education, information, but without it being to the detriment of the other people. The resolution of a conflict by separation is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you have used the term "ethnic cleansing." You're familiar with that term. Did ethnic cleansing occur in the territory occupied by the Bosnian Serb forces in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occupied by the Bosnian Serb forces? I don't know what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll tell you what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did ethnic cleansing occur in the territory in -- under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, listening to your answers to Judge Orie, I am struck by it. Did you defend the rights of Muslims to remain in the territories that now occupy the Republika Srpska, between -- in 1992? Did you defend their rights? Did you assert that they should be permitted to remain in the territory post-April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in fact the case, and could be clearly seen from my public statements. However, I primarily advocated the rights of the Serbs, but in doing so I did not wish to curb the rights of the others. You know, when you make a public statement, the way you formulate what you say is quite important. But the question has several layers to defend under what circumstances, where, and with what resources. In principle, I was in favour of the respect of the rights of all, including the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1992, post-April 1992, to the end of April, what affirmative steps did you take, Mr. Poplasen, to ensure that the Muslim -- Muslims and the Croats living on the territory occupied by the Republika Srpska, would remain in place, particularly the civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which steps could I have taken to begin with? If I met anyone and then I could have asked him whether he was thirsty or hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm asking you what steps you took personally and on behalf of the Serbian Radical Party to ensure that Muslims and Croats, particularly civilians, who lived on the territory occupied by the Bosnian Serb forces, remained in that territory.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the party didn't exist. We have already cleared that up. It was in 1993 that it was registered as a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then let me stand corrected. Let me ask you then, since you were acting on behalf of the Serbian Republican Party, and you told us you were going around Bosnia-Herzegovina, trying to organise the municipal boards of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I think you perfectly understood the question of Mr. Harmon. It was not about when exactly the party was established or when you were preparing the establishment of the party, but what you did do in -- to ensure that the Muslims and Croats, in particular civilians, who lived on the territory of Republika Srpska, to remain in that territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever I had occasion to, I asked for everyone's rights to be respected and tolerated. I otherwise was busy with setting up the boards of the Serb Radical Party. My main priority was the Serb interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example on when and how you asked for such respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are many such examples. I can't recall all of them. I remember, for instance - and I believe this was reported on by the media - that in September 1992, in Banja Luka, at the steering meeting of the board where many people were present, I called all the members of the peoples to respect each other's rights. I called for tolerance and for actions that would reduce violence and destruction on all sides. This was a meeting held in a building called Internacional. There were several hundred people there. There were some people who disliked what I said, but I insisted on that, as did I insist on that in all the meetings. But I did not make note of my statements. I cannot tell you which date it was and who the audience was, I told the Prosecutor already. The better part of my day was spent not running around trying to save the Muslims and the Croats who were at risk, although there were such cases, but rather I focused on setting up boards of the Serb Radical Party. I also had duties as a commissioner. And some refugees. And the day only has 24 hours. And already in November I moved to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you said it was reported by the media. If there would be any way of having that material so that the Chamber could find support for this testimony in that respect, it would certainly be helpful. I'm at this moment -- of course, Mr. Josse, you're blocked but if you would have any of these media reports, could you please -- if you have them, could you please tell us so that we could have a look at them. A similar matter, by the way, Mr. Josse, appears with the reference, for example, the witness made earlier to the double pension legislation. I mean that's all public, I take it. So therefore, the Chamber would very much like to receive such material. I take it, Mr. Harmon, that there would be no problem to providing legal texts so that we could find support for the testimony of the witness in objective documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The double pension issue, in fact, I was personally aware of not via the witness, via other sources. I'm not giving evidence about it, I've been told about it by another source. I'm sure we could verify that and find the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What the witness has just now said, bearing in mind everything the Defence faces, we're almost entirely dependent on the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- frankly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Poplasen, if you would have any press reports on what you just told us, please give a message to us so that we could consider to have a look at it. Please proceed. By the way, it's time for a break anyhow. Could I ask Madam Usher first to escort -- Mr. Poplasen, would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, how much time would you still use -- would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At least one more session and possibly into the following session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider how much time you'll be given. You go well beyond the 60 per cent. At the same time, there is an issue of testimony in rather general and abstract terms and testimony on facts. We'll consider whether you'll get the time you asked for. The Judges might have some questions as well. I'm aware that the Judges have taken already quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are likely to be some short procedural matters which we would like to deal with immediately after the second break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would very much like to finish with the witness today and not any later. I take it, Mr. Josse, that you would have some questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have some at the moment. Not very many, but I do have some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Harmon, would you at least review your programme during the break in order to bring it within the next session and not beyond the next session. Within does not necessarily mean the full time of the next session. And we'll consider -- how much time would the procedural issues take?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Oh, not very long, I assure the Court. One of them I'm learning about as the morning proceeds. Another is a very short matter relating to what Your Honour said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then we'll restart at five minutes past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I see that the witness is already in the courtroom. Would that be any problem in relation to your procedural --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the second break is what I thought I had said, and that's fairly essential, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Harmon, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, yesterday you were asked a question by Mr. Josse at the end of his examination of whether you were aware of the six strategic goals and whether that was something that you were made aware of in any guise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Harmon, I hadn't told you yet but two-thirds of a session would be granted to you. You know how much time that is. At the same time, please keep in mind that the policy of the SRS is not the core of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that evidence in relation to credibility and reliability should find somewhere its end as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You may have noticed I was speaking a little faster than normal, Your Honour. I anticipated your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's always the interpreters who suffer from our rulings. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were asked about the strategic objectives, and your answer was that you -- you said when it came to the document itself, the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me play a video. It will be stand-alone -- I mean it's tape number Extra 2. If we could go to that. It needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1089, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I have a specific question regarding the ruling party. Some opposition parties criticise you for being too close to the ruling party. Would you criticise these opposition parties? What would you say about them? "I would say that they are far away from the Serbian people. You see, when it comes to the ruling party, we have concluded long ago that the Serbian Democratic Party had identified the strategic goals of the Serbian people in an acceptable manner. You see, the Serbian Democratic Party has never given up the uniting of all the Serbian countries on the biggest part of the ethnic ... They have never given up capitalism, that is, non-socialism. They have never given up multi-party system of a parliamentary type. Those are our main goals. It is another thing --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can stop here. We have passed the critical passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, this was an interview that was given by you on the 8th of November 1996. Mr. Poplasen, it is clear from this interview that the substance of the strategic objectives were known to you while you may not have seen the actual document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer the question, of course, but His Honour has promised to grant me 30 seconds to just make an observation. After that, I would immediately answer the question. In my earlier testimony, I heard clearly into the microphone, I don't know if everybody saw it, that someone was -- who was working by the microphones seemed to be working like in a bathroom or something, and I think I heard this comment, and I believe anybody here listening to the Serbian could have heard the comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not fully understand what you mean. Are you saying in your earlier testimony, you heard clearly -- and, of course, we could not see what you heard, but that someone was working by the microphone seemed to be working like in a bathroom. What I noticed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Someone among the interpreters said that I, not somebody else, was doing into the microphone what a person would be doing in a toilet. I cannot really quote the words here, it would be too improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll inquire into the matter, whether any comment was made and which then apparently reached you. And I'll inquire into that matter. It's certainly -- it would be something very unusual. But I'll ask about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be heard on the tape. But let me answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I inquire into it, that could include listening to the tape as well. But at this moment, I take it that we can then continue and that you would answer the last question of Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me reframe the question, Your Honour, so we can move expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you testified you hadn't seen the actual document enunciating the six strategic objectives, but you were aware of their substance, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already commented on that. I talked to Professor Koljevic about what the strategic goals meant, what they implied, and it is quite understandable that the Serb -- the interests of the Serbs were a great priority of mine, that's true, but I didn't see the document, the paper itself that was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One of the goals that they had articulated and identified in an acceptable manner was the establishment of state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I saw the document subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to change the topic. I want to talk about paramilitary formations, Mr. Poplasen. You are aware, are you not, that there was a centre in Belgrade where Mr. Seselj, Mr. Arkan, Mr. Vuk Draskovic, Mr. Mirko Jovic and others gathered volunteers to be sent to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of that is something that I'm fully familiar with. I'm not informed -- I don't know about the details, but in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That centre existed before the commencement of hostilities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that for a fact but I believe that it started operating with the advent of the hostilities in Croatia. As I had been informed about the centre from the media and from conversations, I was never there myself, I never visited the centre. I believe that it existed before the outbreak of the hostilities in Bosnia, at the time of the hostilities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the volunteers who assembled at that location were armed, with the full knowledge and approval of the Serbian authorities, correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the Serbian authorities"? Do you mean Serbia, the Republika Srpska, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia. Slobodan Milosevic was arming those volunteers and his -- well, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As far as I know, they went out into the field without weapons and when they joined the units of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and of the Republic of Serbia when they were assigned to a formation, then they would be given weapons, according to what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me play a film for you. It's found if you turn to tab 47, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has no number yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It has no number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Mr. Poplasen, is a film -- you were present when Mr. Seselj was making these remarks. You were a participant in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Referring, Your Honours, to the top of page 1 in the English of this. If we could play this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]"When we announced you and Mr. Poplasen as guests, many callers called in with questions. However, one question was frequently asked, the question about volunteers and members, as well as sympathisers of your party, who from the day one -- they were present as volunteers on the territories of the former Croatia and former Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nevertheless, the viewers think that this has subsided in time and that even your sympathisers are not interested any more in the future of the Serbs in the Republika Srpska. Is that true? Are your volunteers still there and are you still ready? "That impression is not correct. Our volunteers are still present. There, for example, with the Chetnik Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic at the Jewish cemetery, with Vojvoda Vasko in Ilijas, with Vojvoda Mando Maksimovic on Majevica, as well as a number of volunteers who are with Vojvoda Brne at Ilidza, with Vojvoda Radovic on Podvelezje, and so on and so forth. There are some of them still there. However, there would be more of them if the Command of the Serbian army asked us to send volunteers. It is more difficult for us to send volunteers now than it was in 1991, 1992 and 1993. At the time, when we were sending out volunteers, we had good cooperation with Slobodan Milosevic, who was giving us uniforms, weapons, buses, barracks, such as the Bubanj Potok barracks which was given entirely to the Serbian Radical Party. We had all the necessary equipment. That used to work much better at the time. Because of Slobodan Milosevic's treason --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can stop there. I won't play the rest of the text because of my time limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this dialogue on TV. I don't know where it was but I suppose it was sometime in 1994 that we took part in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The actual date was the 13th of March 1995. But does that refresh your recollection as to the fact that Slobodan Milosevic was providing logistical support to volunteers, including your volunteers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite probable. We had been insisting on this. But it is possible that the weapons arrived through some other channels. The fact is that the volunteers were not armed in Serbia -- our volunteers were not armed in Serbia and then crossed over to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps the weapons arrived through a different channel and then the volunteers were armed the way I told you they were. I'm not saying that all this is true, but Mr. Seselj cooperated with Mr. Milosevic, I didn't have any other information, and I only could believe what Mr. Seselj was saying, and there is no reason for me to disbelieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poplasen, the volunteers that were being provided logistical support in Serbia were welcomed in Bosnia by the Bosnian Serb leadership, by Dr. Karadzic, by Mr. Krajisnik, by Mr. Koljevic, by Mrs. Plavsic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a few minutes then. Let me focus on one paramilitary formation, paramilitary formation that was under the command of Arkan. You knew Arkan, you met Arkan, during the war, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not personal acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, I was about 300 metres away from him, as I was going past with some people. As we were not acquainted with each other, we didn't greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Arkan was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Mr. Poplasen, you say, "I was 300 metres away ..." For me, I always translate it in football grounds. That is three football grounds. If I would see someone at a distance of three football grounds, I would not be able to see who it is. I mean, could you clarify how you say "I was about 300 metres"? Did you see him or were you told that he was at a distance of 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm wearing glasses. I hope they are helping. For several days, Arkan was spending nights in Banja Luka and I was across from him, on the other side of the street, and somebody motioned to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you see him? Did you see a person which you recognised as being Arkan? Apart from a street of 300 metres wide is a rather big street, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to understand what I'm saying. There was a man accompanying me, I don't know who he was. He was, I believe, a police officer, and he pointed to the man on the other side of the square and he told me, There is Arkan passing by Hotel Bosna, and I don't know why I shouldn't have believed the man. That was the only time I saw the man. He was going on his business somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer is someone, he accompanied me, pointed at a man at quite some distance and told me that that was Arkan, but you did not recognise him as such yourself. Is that a correct understanding of your answer? Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.
