utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, Arkan was a notorious criminal before the war started in Bosnia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a criminal. That's for sure. How notorious, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know he was a criminal at the time he was paramilitary leader? Did you know he had been convicted of robberies, that he had been convicted of murders?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew very little of him. I didn't know of the man before the start of the war. When the war started, he was somewhat present in the media. One could hear about him. And as for his background, I found out about it from Mr. Seselj, but I don't know why I would have had to know anything about Arkan from before the war, when he was abroad, involved in some shady deals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit. It is 1090. It's a film clip found in tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I direct Your Honour's attention to the top of -- the bottom of the second page, starting with the word "Seselj." If we could play that portion of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... and other political parties will have a lot of constructive work to do as soon as peace is there. "It is important to address the problem of crime - the problem which most affects the lives of all the Serbs in all the Serbian countries. The main -- all the main criminal activities that have been going on during this war in the territory of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina are linked to the regime in Serbia and the Serbian police. They are also linked to the counter-intelligence service of the army of Yugoslavia in which there are communists, members of the SK for Yugoslavia (we have spoken about that before) and the leaders. For example, Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan, a man of the Serbian UDBA, who used to liquidate immigrants and rob banks in the Western countries. In this war, the press proclaimed him a Serbian hero, although he never had more than two to 300 men under his command. He said that he had liberated Bijeljina. That's not true, because he only had 29 men in Bijeljina. What did he do? He plundered Bijeljina. What did he in do in Brcko? He plundered Brcko. He took away everything he could possibly take. The value of the goods he took can be measured in millions of German marks. He could not have done it by himself. He shipped it with the permission of the Serbian police, Radmilo Bogdanovic, Sokolovic, Radovan Stojisic Badza, and so on and so forth. That was sold on the black market, and the money was shared. He stole even the fire engine from Bijeljina. The whole of Bijeljina was proud of that vehicle; it was worth approximately one and a half million German marks before the war. He drove it over to Erdut, and the vehicle was lost. Such things can never be brought into any relations with the Serbian Radical Party. We are clean, if our past were not so clean, if our activities were not so clean, the regime would already have settled accounts with us. The regime can accuse us of many things, but it cannot prove anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you learn of those facts from Mr. Seselj or did you learn of those facts elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've heard that in that conversation. Perhaps that was the first time that I actually talked about those matters with Mr. Seselj and I have no reason to disbelieve him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you aware and did you get -- were you informed that Mr. Arkan had been involved in the killing of civilians in Bijeljina in early April of 1992? Did you ever hear any reports of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard it subsequently. Now we are talking about it but subsequently, after a number of years, I heard about it. But when all those things were happening in Bijeljina, I had a normal life living and working in Sarajevo. I don't know how I could have gathered that on the basis of summary reports in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you tab -- two photographs very quickly. They are found in tab 61, 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These have exhibit numbers, Your Honour. These are Exhibits P292A for tab 61, and P294B for tab 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at the first picture in tab 61. Have you ever seen that picture before, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen similar pictures. I can't remember this one in particular, but similar pictures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at the related photograph under tab 62. Mr. Poplasen, the Court has heard evidence that these pictures were taken in Bijeljina and that these soldiers depicted in this first photograph are members of Arkan's unit, that those pictures were widely published in the beginning of the war, right after, shortly after the events in Bijeljina. Do you recall seeing those pictures then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't. I've seen very many such photos and I really can't tell you, after 17 years, whether I've seen this particular one. I didn't -- my mind is not a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Had you received -- while you were in Bosnia in 1992 did you receive reports or receive information that Arkan's unit was involved in killing civilians?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would give me some information or any reports? I was in the opposition. Nobody was duty bound to provide me with any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you're not asked whether someone could have given it and whether it would be logical for you to receive. The question simply was whether you received reports or received information. Not whether anyone was under an obligation to provide it to you but just whether you received it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- I mean, the way it was translated to me was, Did you receive a report? In Serbian language, it implies that there is a formal channel through which somebody either orally or in writing, according to a system of subordination, would submit a report to me. But I said that I was informed through the media, like all the other citizens, but in a very summary fashion, because there were no such pictures shown in the media and there were no descriptions of the killings of civilians and so on. But I'm not saying that this hasn't happened. I just didn't have insight into that and I didn't know Arkan and I didn't know that he was coming to Bijeljina. I saw on TV that Mrs. Plavsic went to visit Bijeljina and that she met with Arkan and greeted him, et cetera, but, yesterday I said that in many things she was more radical than I was, but I didn't get any more information than your average man in the street back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- you received information by watching television. Any other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presumably in the papers as well. I used to read the papers too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall any other source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did those sources of information that you had in 1992 disclose that Arkan had been involved in the killing of civilians in operations in which he participated?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It was presented as a kind of interethnic conflict in Bijeljina, as far as I can remember. But you can find that information in the news broadcasts of the BH television. And as a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the camera was actually zooming in on Mrs. Plavsic, and she went to Bijeljina and those events did appear rather dramatic. There were reports of shooting, but I don't remember anyone saying volunteers came from Serbia and killed civilians in Bijeljina. Certainly nobody put it in quite those terms. So there was description of these dramatic events but I would really have to watch that tape once again. That would probably jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's quite all right. I want to talk about volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party. If we could -- first of all I want to ask you a couple of questions about their presence. There were a number of volunteers who formed under the guidance of the Serbian Radical Party in Bosnia. That's a correct statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could take a look at a film. It needs an exhibit number. It is to be found in tab 41. This, for your information, Mr. Poplasen, we are going to be looking at a film that's in two parts. One is of a ceremony that took place where 18 new Chetnik vojvodas were honoured, given the designation of vojvoda. And the second part is a part where you participated with Mr. Seselj shortly after that ceremony in Sokolac, and your image will appear in it. So if we could play that film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 41 will be P1091.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Today on the first day of the referendum, Dr. Vojislav Seselj arrived at the Republika Srpska. He's the Chetnik vojvoda and the president of the Serb Radical Party. Right after crossing the Drina he went to visit our defenders on the defence lines. After this, he visited Knezina, the village and monastery in free Serbian Romanija. An oath-taking for new Serbian Chetnik vojvodas. "Order number 124. As the only Serbian Chetnik vojvoda who was directly engaged in the present liberating struggle of the Serbian people by following the tradition of Serbian Chetniks for extraordinary service in this war, the great heroism and combat skills of the most outstanding Chetnik commanders I declare ... "So new 18 Romanija, a mountain that will not negotiate with enemies, I was glad to see the oath-taking of the new 18 vojvodas. It is an oath that's not been heard for 50 years. "I do solemnly declare that as a Serbian Chetnik vojvoda ... "I declare before God and Sveti Sava ... "I declare before God and Sveti Sava ... "That I shall fight with all my strength for the freedom of the Serbian people ... "That I shall fight with all my strength for the freedom of the Serbian people ... "And for the renewal of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans that will include all Serbian lands ... "And for the renewal of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans that will include all Serbian lands ... "So help me God. "So help me God. "Amen. "Amen. "They can be trusted that it will be so. The following Serbian heroes from all parts of Serb lands were given the rank of Chetnik vojvoda: Zdravko Abramovic, Branislav Vakic, Srecko Radovanovic, Slavko Crnic, Nedeljko Vidakovic, Slavko Aleksic, Mitar Maksimovic - Manda, Miroslav Vukovic - Cele, Milika Dacevic - Ceko, Tomislav Nikolic, Milan Lancuzanin - Kameni, Zoran Drazinovic - Cica, Jovo Ostojic, Ljubisa Petkovic, Todor Lazic, Mirko Blagojevic, Dragan Cvetkovic and Branislav Gavrilovic - Brne. "Brne! Brne! Turn around a bit so I can get a good shot. Hey, that's good. "And then Sokolac."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are going to stop right there. Just for Your Honour's benefit and for counsel's benefit, the man who has been identified as Brne, there has been other evidence in this Chamber. I refer Your Honours to intercepted radio communication, telephone communication, I should say, Prosecution Exhibit 292, KID 31208, an intercept from April, between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Gavrilovic. Now we can continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The image on the right-hand side, the man on the right with the beard, that's you, isn't it, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "If there is a military intervention, thousands and thousands of our volunteers will cross the Drina to be here with you. All of us that you can see here today, we'll all be here amongst you and share your destiny. "After the rally, Mr. Seselj went to Pale esorted by the newly-appointed vojvodas to talk with the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me -- did you accompany Dr. Seselj to meet with Dr. Karadzic in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I must have done, but there were a number of such visits, and within a brief period of time. When Mr. Seselj was in the Republika Srpska, most often I was together with him, unless I had other duties which were -- I considered to be more of a priority but most often I would be with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 42, this needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 42, Your Honours, will be 1092.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document does not have a translation. For your benefit, Mr. Poplasen, I will read it into the record. It's dated the 15th of May. It's from Tanjug news service. "Dr. Vojislav Seselj, chairman of the Serbian Radical Party, began talks today with the leadership of the Serb republic ... in Pale. "The talks are attended by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the Serb Republic; Nikola Koljevic, vice-president of the Serb Republic; Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Serb Republic Assembly; and Nikola Poplasen, chairman of the Serb Radical Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina. "As has been learned, they are discussing new political possibilities for a peaceful solution to the crisis in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Seselj arrived in Pale after visiting Knezina and Sokoc." During those discussions, Mr. Poplasen, the -- Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic and others with whom you were speaking were fully informed of the presence of volunteers from the Serb Radical Party, the presence of the 18 new vojvodas. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean in its entirety, or fully? It was probably one of the topics. Probably one of the topics was also the sending of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next image, which will be -- it's from the same -- this is from the same exhibit number, so it's 1092. This is a brief clip of a public address by Mr. Seselj and Dr. Karadzic. So if we could play that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Republic of Yugoslavia apart from the representatives of the Serbian Orthodox Church no comments could be heard by the officials in the RS ... however Dr. Vojislav Seselj, the leader of the strongest opposition party in Serbia, the SRS, wanted to strengthen the support to the people and the leadership of the RS by coming to Sokolac and to Pale. Dr. Vojislav Seselj and the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, gave the following statements to Channel S after today's meeting. "I would just like to say in our language that we are very honoured by this visit of Mr. Seselj and his associates, especially since it's taking place at the time of our referendum, which is of great importance to us and for which we have gained the support of the radical ... of the SRS and Mr. Seselj. We do have a habit of meeting occasionally and in the future we'll try and meet with all the other leaders of all parliamentary parties in Serbia and Montenegro, that is Yugoslavia, and to continue cooperation. Some of them are very close to us, some less so, but that is exactly the reason why we have to maintain dialogue with all of them. "The delegation of the SRS, the biggest opposition party in the FRY and second in power in that state, is visiting the Republika Srpska today and we have been received by the president of this republic. We came here to visit a few Serbian towns, to visit Serbian soldiers on their positions, to meet with the people and to follow the referendum that's taking place because we feel that this referendum is of great existential importance for the Serbian people here and the SRS is following its rule, its principle that the Serbian people here must be the sole masters of their own destiny and that all outside political subjects must respect the inviolability of its will and the legitimacy of decisions passed by its governmental organs and the decisions that the people themselves passed through the referendum. I'm convinced that the people of the RS will reject the Vance Owen Plan because that plan opposes its national interests, its vital and existential interests and not because somebody will convince the people to reject the plan. Were this plan good for the Serbian people, it would be futile to try and convince the people to reject it."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me then go to the next exhibit. It's found in tab 48. Mr. Poplasen, this is a regular combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It's dated 18 April 1992 and I would like to direct your attention to subpart 3, which I will read into the record. It is -- this report is also signed by the commander, Stanislav Galic. "3. The situation in the territory without significant changes. However, a paramilitary formation consisting of about 25 men commanded by Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, is active in the Rakovica sector. This is a group of criminals whose behaviour is damaging the reputation of the Republika Srpska in the eyes of the population in this territory." I invite your comments, your brief comments, as to commander Galic's observations of Mr. Gavrilovic. Did you hear of such reports?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard of this report. This is the first time I've set eyes on it and I have no reason at all to doubt the assessment of Mr. Galic because he's a very serious and conscientious man. Probably it's about the following. Probably Mr. Seselj had been informed of this. I do remember -- I can't remember the exact date but I do remember that because of this, we made a special trip to Ilidza to see the brigade commander to clarify the matter. Mr. Seselj talked to Gavrilovic to warn him of that sort of behaviour and to tell him that he had to subject himself to the brigade command, and everything in this respect had to be considered by the command and dealt with. There were quite a few of us there on that occasion, and the meeting took place at Ilidza. There were some ten of us and we talked to the brigade commander at his command and then we went to this location that is referred to here at Rakovica to see Gavrilovic, and Mr. Seselj talked to him. Mr. Gavrilovic at that stage didn't like me for some reason, so I wasn't in a position myself to talk to him directly, but I'm absolutely certain that Mr. Seselj discussed this topic with him for quite sometime and brought quite some pressure to bear in order for this to be dealt with, and it took place at the so-called Orchard Centre at Rakovica. There were those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that meeting with Mr. Seselj and Mr. Gavrilovic took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it should have been by the end of 1992, the beginning of 1993. I can't recall the exact date. I suppose that the contents of this information somehow reached Mr. Seselj and that he had been warned of this, because there was a clear party rule that there should be no units anywhere outside the framework of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, no independent units which would not be subject to the regular command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if I were to inform you that by at least February the 12th, 1993, Mr. Gavrilovic was still not subordinated to the VRS, will you accept that fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. It is possible. But I don't have full insight into the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn very quickly - I don't want to spend very much time on this - but tab 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 48, Your Honours, P1093.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 51?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 51 will be P1094.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 12th of February 1993, and at the bottom there is a signature of Srdjan Sehovac. It's an official note from the Minister of the Interior, National Security Service, the Ilidza war department. And it says, in the second paragraph: "With the arrival of the new commander, Captain Spasoje Cajic, Brne's formation felt it would not have the privileges it had had until that time and that it would have to place itself under the brigade command; i.e., as an integral part of the Republika Srpska army. Upon the arrival of the new commander, Brne came in person to him and told him he knew everything about him, including the exact time he was to take over the brigade, and one of the Chetniks had told him that he was in charge of his liquidation. Owing to this wisdom and composure of the said colonel, a 'temporary' common ground was found with aka Brne's men, but this is still far from true subordination to the superior command." I won't read further. So does that give you any reason to dispute that particular date and time at which point Mr. Gavrilovic was no longer under -- was not under the command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific reasons to dispute what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to tab 55 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, let me just inquire into what kind of evidence we are hearing at this moment. The evidence presented, the swearing in of new vojvodas, among them Brne, now we see that Brne, at least on the basis of your documentation, is suggested to have behaved in an undisciplinary way and -- what is exactly what we are heading for? Is it that you would say that this witness, by being present at the swearing-in, supported this kind of irregular -- irregular armed forces or people? Is that it? Or what are we heading for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I intend to ask some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I would like very much to keep in mind that this is not a case against the SRS or against this witness, but that I'm still wondering where the links, the direct links -- of course, there are always some links but whether they are direct and strong links with the case we are hearing. But please proceed, but keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, some of the links, Your Honour, will become apparent with future witnesses as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's always a problem for a Chamber that we never can see where we are heading, and sometimes after half an hour or after five days we say, well, it was an excellent way of doing it, and sometimes after a couple of hours or after a couple of days, we say why did we have to hear all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if you could turn to tab 55, please. Mr. Poplasen, this is a Serbian Radical Party war staff authorisation, dated the 13th of December 1991, from Belgrade, and it is signed by Chief Ljubisa Petkovic. Do you recognise that name and the signature at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the name, but how should I know his signature? I know the person. I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is an authorisation to permit a gentleman by the name of Nikodin Cavic from Banja Luka to sign up volunteers from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina without special permission, and on the basis of written request and signatures of authorised officials. And he was then to screen these people, and the text goes on. Do you know Mr. Cavic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with him -- or rather, met him, on several occasions. We were not close acquaintances, though, and unfortunately he passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he was authorised by the Serbian Radical Party to sign up volunteers in Banja Luka, according to this document. And he did so, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, he did. Of course, this is the first time I set my eyes on this document. This is the year 1991, and I didn't know of the existence of the staff. At the time, I didn't know this man. I met him later. At this particular period of time, I was living and working in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can this have an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 51, Your Honours, will be P1095. 55, Your Honours, tab 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's now corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, were any of the people who were identified as 18 new vojvodas ever disciplined by the Serbian Radical Party for criminal conduct that had occurred in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number of them. I can't recall all of their names, but I could supply you with the information subsequently. One of them was not only found responsible but was expelled from the party, which was the highest discipline that could -- measure that could be applied. And from the staff, some information came about the persons who should even be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What type of crimes are we talking about, in summary form?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to try and find the papers. Probably it involved fights, wounding, something of the sort that was incompatible with the work of the Serb Radical Party. There must be some documentation somewhere but I would have to look into that and supply you with it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it include crimes committed against Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. There were some offences. I don't remember which. I had no authority whatsoever over the vojvodas. That was within the purview of the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So your answer is you don't know if it involved crimes committed against Muslim civilians? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- we can't go further with that topic if you can't recall more than that, Mr. Poplasen. Let me turn to another topic quickly. That is the prison in Vogosca. You testified about that. You testified about a location, Sonja's. In fact, you felt that the conditions in that prison were inadequate because there was insufficient food and overcrowding. And you made your concerns known on a number of occasions to the RS authorities, the Republika Srpska authorities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, you wrote a number of letters to the Republika Srpska authorities, complaining about the conditions that you found in that camp. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't complain. I asked that the conditions change, that it be legalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the -- your testimony the other day was that you asked either that it be legalised, the prison, either be disbanded or integrated into the prison system. I think that was your testimony. Your Honours, that's found at page 62 of the transcript. Correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the people who were being detained in that location were civilians, Muslim civilians I think was your evidence.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the -- they, to Mr. Koljevic or the authorities above you, that those people should be released from prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed them not only orally but in writing as well, as I've said. I wrote a letter to the minister of justice, a copy was sent to Mr. Koljevic, wherein I asked that the people be treated in keeping with the law and that what was termed by Vlac [phoen] as detention to be integrated into the judicial, that's the prison system, and that the operation of this facility be legalised. In view of the fact that the situation with the food in this facility and at Vogosca was inadequate, I asked that adequate food supplies be ensured. This visit, which lasted some 15 to 20 minutes, was the only visit to this facility and yielded the results that I have just relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you a very specific question: Did you ask Mr. Koljevic to have the civilians in that prison released from custody?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This goes without saying. A person cannot be held in a prison if there are no legal bases for his being there. When I said that I wanted the facility to be integrated into the prison system, what did I want to say by this? I see a Muslim walking on the street, I seize him and take him and lock him up in a facility. That's why I'm saying there has to be a legal basis for him being detained, which, of course, triggers a certain legal procedure, which has to have its end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the response of Dr. Koljevic to that information that you had given him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He agreed with that. I told him that I had sent the letter to the minister of justice and the Deputy Prime Minister. He said that was a good thing to do and I will talk to them about it. I then went on some other business away. I believed that this was discussed by the government, that this was in fact put on the government's agenda, but, of course, I was not a cabinet member and I can't know whether they in fact discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were the Muslim civilians from Sonja's house released, after that discussion with Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I to know this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, you might know it because you were a commissioner in the municipality and it was an area that was of interest to you and you had raised it at the highest levels of government. That's how you might know about it. So my question is were they released after you had raised this issue with Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was whether the Muslim civilians had been released. I didn't say that there weren't any other civilians, Serbs and Croats and so on and so forth. How am I to know whether some Croats and Serbs were kept behind when some Muslim civilians were released? I find the question quite strange. Based on the information that was given to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, let's not discuss the question. The question simply is you took initiatives to have people released. The question was were they released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I launched this initiative and procedure for them to be released. Whether this was in fact done, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A follow-up was not your interest? I mean, if I'm interested in the fate of people that may be illegally detained, and I take steps to get them released, then usually one would wonder to know whether these steps were successful. Could you explain to us why you did not give that any follow-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was convinced that the local authorities and the republican authorities would do their jobs according to law. There were other places where there were similar dramatic situations and it is quite impossible to double check all that. It's not the absence of interest for human life but rather the faith and belief that the people acted in accordance with their duties, with the law, whereby a person committing a crime needs to be held responsible. And how was I able to go and -- from house to house to check whether this was in fact done, whether there had been a follow-up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it would not have needed to go house to house. You could have just asked the prison warden whether the people were released, isn't it? It takes you five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I asked the president of the municipal government about it and he told me that all was well. Why would I have to go and ask the prison warden about it? I have nothing to do with him. I was not his superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he say that they were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the Executive Board of the municipality told me that the proceedings were in course in keeping with the law, and I believed the facility, the prison, to have been integrated into the system which had existed in Sarajevo before the war, which had the necessary staff and experience, that they had the premises they needed and they had procedure in place. I thought the problem solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to show you three documents, Mr. Poplasen. If we could turn first of all to tab 27. If I could get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 27 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, 27 has a number. 29, if I could have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 29 will be P1096.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. If I could have a number for tab 28.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 28 will be P1096, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, if we could first of all turn to tab 27, Mr. Poplasen. It is tab 27. It's P743 is the exhibit number. Mr. Poplasen, this is a document from the Vogosca Serbian Municipality War Commission, dated the 6th of August 1992. It's a conclusion, and the conclusion, the -- "That approval is asked from the aforementioned addressee for occasional use of detainees for construction and other work, according to the current needs." Now, this document is signed apparently on your behalf. You see the signature on the original document that says for you? Do you recognise this document? Do you remember this document being signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but there is no reason for me to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at, then, the document that is found in tab 29. This is Exhibit 455. This is from the War Commission to the Ministry of Justice. It is type-signed as coming from the president of the Serbian Municipality of Vogosca, and it asks the Ministry of Justice for the very same request; that is, the use of detained persons in construction work and other works as the need arises. And then finally, if we turn to tab 28, Mr. Poplasen, this is now Exhibit 1096, this is -- appears to be the response from the Ministry of Justice, dated the 10th of August 1992, and it is -- bears a typed signature of Momcilo Mandic. It has a reference number, and it says: "Regarding your request for the engagement of detainees in works, we hereby inform you that we are in agreement that detainees be temporarily engaged in construction and other works." Now, the term "construction and other works," Mr. Poplasen, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I to know? Probably some construction work, repairing buildings that were damaged in shelling, or repairs of the roads; whatever constitutes construction work. As for under "other works," I suppose that of whatever needed to be delivered or carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it mean that these prisoners who were in custody of the prison authorities were to be released to work on front line positions, for example, digging trenches, building defensive fortifications?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not informed about this, although this term "lines" can be stretched quite far, because the whole town could be the line, the front line, and then, of course, if the -- depending on what the emphasis of the attacks or the fighting was, the line moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a republican commissioner, did you hear that in the Vogosca municipality, civilians who had been prisoners were forced to work at front line positions where combat was occurring?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a republican commissioner, one can see from the last few documents that you have admitted into evidence that the commission insisted on legality. We are addressing the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Justice does not in turn address the commission but the local authorities. Our goal was to ensure that the activities were conducted in keeping with the law. Of course, everything was happening in a state of war. If there are bodies that are not working in keeping with the law, then there are inspection services and other service to monitor the work. It wasn't the duty of the commission to do that. Our duty was to ensure that the authorities that were legally elected did their job properly. If their activities included some of the activities you've mentioned now, then they should have been held liable under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So what you're saying, Mr. Poplasen, is the use of civilian prisoners at -- in construction activities and other work at dangerous front line positions where they could be wounded or killed would be illegal. It would be a crime. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose we should look into the regulations covering that, but detainees often have a duty to do some work, but I don't suppose there is meant to be put in a position where their lives are at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Poplasen. I have a difficulty because I can't follow you any more in your explanations. Yesterday you gave us a description of the role of the commissioner. You told us that the commissioner was there to see whether decisions taken by local authorities would be legal. I think you underscored the fact that you had no decision power on such matters, and then you explained to us, if I remember you rightly, that after that you had delegated your own monitoring authority, as far as legality is concerned, to commissioners, to people who were sort of subcommittee and that the subcommittee had the same role as yourself, which was one again to monitor and appraise the legality of the decisions taken by the local authorities. And in your explanations this morning, and through the documents which have been presented, we have the impression that there was a committee called War Committee which existed, which you seemed to be leading and which is taking decisions instead of the local authorities. So could you clarify all this. Because any way, as far as I'm concerned, perhaps I'm not clever enough to understand, but I get the impression that we are seeing something more and more confused. Was there - yes or no - a War Commission which substituted itself to the local authorities and who was able to make decisions, to write directly to the ministry, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the setting up of the commission, there used to be a body which was called the Crisis Staff, and those Crisis Staffs were abolished on the basis of a Presidency decision, and the municipal commission, following a proposal from the republic commissioner, and there we've got the decision that I signed, and all the other bodies would continue in existence and would continue operating in line with the law. It is indeed true that for a certain period of time the so-called Crisis Staffs used to exist, but here we are talking about the period of time in which I was not really active and I was not present or active either in Vogosca or in any other municipality. We are talking about April, May and June. So now we've got the category -- I can see why you're puzzled, because most citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be puzzled as well, because there were the legal authorities, the Municipal Assembly, the Crisis Staffs, the commission, and then something else which was called the War Presidency, either by mistake or rightly so, but all this is rather puzzling. However, the whole point of my work, or the whole point of the setting up of the commission was to ensure that the legal institutions' role be upgraded as much as possible and that only the necessary rectifications be made through the commission. And in May, June, July, as time passed, I could see that more and more Tribunals were being set up and the administrative bodies, and so that vacuum that existed at the very beginning of the war had been overcome, so all these positions were becoming staffed gradually, and so the conditions were being created in order for all that to start operating. And I did say yesterday that I accepted the role of commissioner precisely in order to promote and speed up the creation of all the legal institutions and bodies. Of course, if there was a whole range of extreme and unacceptable situations, and even crimes, and the Prosecution does point out to them, but they had to be dealt with according to the provisions of the law. What was unacceptable to me was to make decisions on behalf of somebody else. In this case, my decision was signed by somebody else on my behalf, by Ratko Babic in this instance, but I did tell him do not make any decisions which are within the area of competence of somebody else. Now, this seems like a simple task. He would have to turn to the Justice Ministry, and the Justice Ministry did not tell the commission anything. They got in touch with the president of the Municipal Assembly, and he was the one who was to ensure that everything was done through the proper channels. So we did not have a well-established system or model of controls a postiori and feedback, and so that was the problem. I don't know whether I've been of any assistance with this explanation, but that's the way I understood it, and it is for this reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To ensure this monitoring of the legality of what the local authorities were doing, did you consider that you had to go on the site to see what was going on, to make sure that things were happening legally, were being done legally? How could you check whether decisions were legal if you didn't go and check on-site, on the different sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said earlier that the decisions were implemented and checked by the legal bodies, enshrined in law. There were inspections and inspectors within the Justice Ministry and it was up to them to establish whether the ministry's decision was implemented properly. In the last analysis, there is a possibility of somebody swindling me. Because I did not have the necessary professional expertise, they might have just swindled me and make me believe that things had been done properly when they had not. And that's why I wanted for the municipal leadership to be informed, because that's where my role was exhausted. I wanted to get some feedback there. And in case I found out that what I got from them in terms of feedback did not correspond to the situation on the ground, I would have had to react, but then I had other problems in that case. Perhaps I should have gone to the hospitals as well and visit whether Muslims and Serbs and Croats were all treated in the same way. I should have perhaps visited the schools as well. Life is a complex matter and there is always somebody who makes a decision, somebody who implements them, et cetera, but I take it that people also have to have some trust and confidence. Why should I work on the assumption that every time the president of the Executive Board or the president of the Municipal Assembly or the police chief, every time they come and tell me something are telling me lies, or somebody from the ministry? In case they are all telling lies it is a very pessimistic, disastrous, chaotic situation. It could be impossible for any life to take place there. According to that principle of chain of responsibility you could ask the president of the republic why, in some village 500 kilometres away, a sick man died and he was not provided with proper assistance, because he would be held accountable for everything. Maybe the nurse had not arrived on time, and it is all regulated by relevant regulations. We know who is to be held accountable, and this chain of accountability, as you seem to be presenting it, I really don't see how it can function in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poplasen, a last question -- my last question, anyway. For you, was the fact of being deprived freedom of your citizens, if it wasn't legal, was this for you a particularly important crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions in this respect as well, and then we'll have a break anyhow. Mr. Poplasen, you explained to us that once you experienced that civilians were held, detained, without a proper basis, as far as I understand, that you reported this as something that should be taken care of and that it should all be legalised. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I address the parties at this moment. Are there any documents found? Because we have some Vogosca documents in which a written report was sent to the minister of -- Ministry of Justice or to whatever authority because it would be exculpatory certainly, Mr. Harmon. Has it been found? Has it been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Bear with me one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll leave you some time. Of course, Mr. Josse the next question, if it would have been confirmed, if it would have been disclosed, then of course the Chamber would like to see such exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I assumed it did not exist because I assumed I would have received it if it had, but it may be a very foolish assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I give Mr. Harmon a minute's time to try to find that out, or perhaps during the break. At the same time, Mr. Poplasen, you, who was so concerned about illegal detention of civilians, your War Commission, on the 6th of August asks permission to use detainees for construction and other works. Did you verify whether these detainees which were needed for work, whether they were civilians or not and whether they were legally detained or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that subsequently I asked the president of the Executive Board whether everything was done in line with the legal provisions, and he replied in the affirmative. And so, generally speaking, I did ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Generally speaking, you did. When did you write that letter asking for the release of civilian detainees? When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I arrive at Vogosca by the beginning of July, I must have gone there in the beginning and as soon as I saw the situation I would have written the letter and sent it off. I can't remember the exact date but it would have been in the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Somewhere in July. You said you arrived in the beginning of July, so it must have been somewhere in July. Now, the 6th of August, did you receive firm confirmation of the matter being resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am not sure I was at Vogosca on the 6th of August. I think I was with my family in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether at the 6th of August you were in Vogosca. I asked you whether by that date, wherever you were, you had received firm confirmation of the matter being resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had not received any firm confirmation in the form of a certain detailed report, if that's what you mean by firm confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Firm confirmation" is that you received information not that everything went well or that one was working on it or that one was making good progress, but here it would mean that the illegal situation would have ended. And then if people were illegally detained, that, of course, would include that they would have been released. Because otherwise the illegal situation would continue to exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The information that I received from the president of the Executive Board was not just a single sentence. Well, he said, "We are doing it in line with the law. We are solving the problem of starvation and we are having difficulties in terms of space and quite a few people -- as far as I could understand, some Muslims wanted to feel safe in some enclosed area until they could be taken somewhere else, so it was a whole range of problems that I was told about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. If you say they are working on space and they are working on starvation, that, of course, is not a real solution for illegal detention, would it? Because if you're illegally detained, one should release you and then space is not a problem any more. It might even improve. Starvation would be the problem of the civilian himself and not your concern any more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that he confirmed that they were working in line with the legal provisions. That would mean that nobody was unlawfully detained, I suppose, if you work in line with the legal provisions. None of the civilians can be detained unless there is some reason for it, some legal basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But a couple of weeks before that, the situation was certainly different. They were not aware of their obligation not to illegally detain civilians. What made you believe that after a couple of weeks, the situation on these kind of vague notions, because they said it's in line with the law, et cetera, no one ever said to you, "We've released them," did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all the attitude of the Justice Ministry and the clear report, or rather, information from the president of the local government, the municipal government, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether anyone told you, "We released them."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in early August, permission is asked for sending detainees for construction and other works. Was it verified at that moment whether these could include illegally detained civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I say in early August, permission is asked to use detainees for construction and other work Vogosca detainees, request submitted by the Vogosca prison warden. Did you or did the War Commission verify whether those detainees who they wished to be allowed to send to work, whether that still would include or could include illegally detained civilians? Did you verify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period of time, I wasn't in Vogosca, as I mentioned earlier on, and that's why somebody else signed it on my behalf, and I think you should ask the person who signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When were you back in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose after ten weeks, up to a fortnight, because I had a great deal to do with my family.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 10 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So by mid-August, you would be back, being the main responsible person as a republican commissioner. Did you view at what had happened in your absence, or did you receive reports; we asked for permission to get people to work and we got that permission or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not told about any details. Of course, I met the other members of the commission, the president of the Executive Board, and I think I must have stayed in Vogosca for a day or two, and then I must have gone somewhere else on some party business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I'm interested to know whether, upon your return, the issue of getting permission to send detainees to work, whether that came to you, that information, and the decision that they could be sent there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember about this actual problem having been mentioned at all. I can't really tell, but I do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received evidence that detainees, civilian detainees, held without any form of process, were sent -- were still detained in that period and were sent to the front lines. This Chamber also received evidence that the death of some of those prisoners or injuries of those prisoners was reported by the -- by the armed forces. Would you have any comment on that evidence this Chamber has received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry if that's the case and I'm sorry about the victims, but I really do not have any information in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the location of where those people would have to do their construction and other work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said construction would have been something like. Were you informed about any specific object on which the detainees would work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Harmon, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I could respond to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can respond to Your Honour's earlier inquiry. We are not in possession of any letter asking for the release of detainees. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has there been a -- well, could I say more or less full review of Vogosca documents in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There has, Your Honour. The closest document I have is found in tab 32. It only relates to the testimony of the witness who testified, as I recall, at page 62 that he had either asked that the facility be disbanded, and I took for granted civilians be released, or that it be integrated into the prison system. There is only one document. It's found at tab 32, and the only request from Mr. Poplasen is that the prison be essentially integrated. I can confront the witness with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would say no request for release but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is no request for release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Poplasen, we will have a break. You are, however, invited, in order to better enable us to inquire into the issue you raised before - let's say the bathroom incident - whether you would remember when approximately or at what moment approximately this was said. If you remember, for example, the question you were answering at that time or the answers you were giving when you heard this, this would assist the Chamber, and -- if you know at this moment. We could take -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was when apparently there was some technical problem. You raised the issue of the microphone and it is at that stage that I heard it through my headphones. As to whether everyone heard it or not, I do not know but that's what I did hear through my headphones. You were commenting on some technical problem with the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, just -- I need to correct something I said about the material that Mr. Harmon's been looking for. I said I assumed it did not exist. Of course, what I meant is it doesn't presently exist. In other words, I have to correct my own English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes you have to assume that it presently does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was not impeaching my own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And even -- yes. I fully understand that. That's how I understood it, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I really need to get my English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not available to us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I really need to get my English right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll think about my Dutch one of these days, Mr. Josse. We'll have a break until quarter past one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, I see you there. Mr. Josse asked for some limited time for a procedural matter. Are you dealing with the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Sorry, which matter are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are a number of different matters. Mr. Josse is dealing with the particular point that arose. Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm just not clear which matter we are talking about. I apologise, Your Honour, I hadn't realised that the matter which I did come to deal with had been touched upon before. But never mind, I'll start from scratch. Your Honour, we are running into difficulty about witnesses next week. I received information this morning from the Victims and Witnesses Section that Mr. Arsovic [phoen], who was due to give evidence as the second witness next week, has a -- well, he has a medical problem, Your Honour. There is no need for me to go into that. I can certainly say that. He has a medical problem which has been reported to me which, as I understand, at least prevents him from travelling. I'm having inquiries made as to find out whether that prevents him from giving evidence, wherever he is, but my understanding on very recent information obtained through my team is that, yes, he is quite ill at the moment. This apparently is going to be the position for a week or two. That's as much as I've been able to establish at the moment, Your Honours. So that's -- that is an obvious problem for next week. Your Honour, we don't -- we can't, in practice, have backup witnesses for specific dates. Your Honour will understand. It just doesn't and can't work like that, so the position we are in is that it's Mr. Radojko who is programmed to give evidence on Monday, we would expect that his evidence would finish, all being well, sometime on Tuesday. Most of these witnesses, as Your Honours would have seen, take, broadly speaking, two days for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. That leaves us in the position, Your Honour, where, come Wednesday next week there is no practical prospect of having a witness here and prepared to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the circumstances -- well, not seeking, in a sense, to take advantage of this unfortunate situation but simply looking to be practical and make the best of a difficult situation, we were already on the Defence side placed with enormous difficulties as far as Mr. Radojko is concerned, whom we've never seen and never spoken to. Not the ideal situation, but we were, of course, to fit in with the proposed schedule, absolutely doing our best and proceeding on the footing that we would, the Court sitting in the afternoons next week, start with Mr. Radojko according to the programme on Monday. However, Your Honour, if there is an inevitability of there being days next week when the Court simply cannot sit because of the -- I say cannot sit, Your Honours understand what I mean -- where we won't have witnesses because of the difficulties which I've suggested, it is the Defence's request, therefore, that one of those days could, and in our submission should, usefully be Monday because then we can valuably use Monday for further preparation of Mr. Radojko. Starting from the position, Your Honour, that the preparation which we had built into the witness programme as planned was not seriously adequate from our point of view. It was just the best we could do. So, Your Honour, that's a report. Of course, I can -- that's as much as I know, effectively, but Your Honours, of course, any questions Your Honours address to me in relation to these witness difficulties I would do absolutely my best to answer. But that's a report coupled with a submission and an application as to how to proceed with the next immediate witness in the light of the practical situation that we have in relation to what was going to be the following witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which witness would have been the following one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Arsovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has he a passport?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he has. I've seen a copy of his passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has he applied for a visa already?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my understanding is that all the normal practical matters had been taken care of in a perfectly regular way, that there was no problem about visa, no problem about security, no problem about clearance. The only obstacle has been this news about his medical condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would prefer to have the next witness in line here as soon as possible. That's the simple answer. Of course, I do not know whether tickets are already ordered for a later date but whether they could be changed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For whom, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next witness you would expect. You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, please understand, Your Honour. We have certainly -- we would not have done, and the implication that we might have done I'm afraid I resist. No, of course we have not taken any such pre-emptive action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now asking you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- straightaway and remained with the perfectly efficient arrangements we'd made as they have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you are now invited to see whether it would be possible to have the next witness in The Hague as soon as possible so that we would not lose any additional --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one you said was next on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Absolutely -- Your Honour is now talking about the witness Radojko who we had scheduled and still have scheduled, as things stand, for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the next one was not available, from what I understand for health reasons, so there would be someone after that one, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's that I started off. Your Honour, of course we will do, as I assure Your Honour we do do, we will do anything and everything we can, but I'm informing Your Honour conscientiously about the practical position that I see no serious prospect whatever of being able to accelerate a later witness in our programme to be ready to give evidence at the time that Mr. Arsovic would have given evidence, in other words immediately after Mr. Radojko. It's only right that I should tell Your Honours. It's not in an uncooperative spirit, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about cooperation, but has the next witness in line, has he been invited to come to The Hague and to start testimony next Wednesday or Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, for this reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I explain? Since Your Honour asked me, I said I would deal with any questions. First of all, this has happened this morning. We do our best, Your Honour. We make telephone calls, which we have done; we make inquiries, which we have done. Mr. Josse has been in court this morning. There are limits. However, we have actually made all the inquiries we could reasonably have done. So far as the next witness in line is concerned, all I can tell Your Honour is that we are already, and we know we are, and we have done already, running into enormous difficulty with that witness. The question to that witness, can you come earlier, would, without going into too much detail, have been a completely pointless question. We are running into the question of whether that witness can and will come at the date when we planned for that witness to come. It would have been a futile question to have said to the witness, can you come earlier? So we haven't asked that question, Your Honour, and won't ask it, with respect, at any time when it is pointless to ask it because we are just going through the motions of futile questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the one after that? I mean, Mr. Stewart, the problem is the following: You've asked for delay -- for further time to prepare and sometimes you said it's to prepare for the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik, and in the beginning, that was not the issue, but you would need further preparations. Now we are confronted with a situation where a witness cannot appear -- cannot appear and that you more or less tell us this witness comes to The Hague, we've never seen him before, we've never spoken to him before. So there seems to be nothing of preparation and this Chamber has given a scheduling order in which limited time is granted, and I emphasise again and again that this Chamber wants to hear as much relevant evidence as it -- as is possible. And the Chamber will not just accept that we say, well -- of course, it can happen that a witness is ill and he can't come. It can happen that a family member of a witness is ill or deceases, but just accepting so we have not resolved the matters for next week, we are under time restraints and we have to do everything possible to have witnesses here so that the Chamber can receive that evidence. This is the basic line, and what it takes of being inventive, changing schedules, trying to find other solutions, that's all to be done to the best. And, of course, then finally if you say, well, we didn't manage to do that, we come to the very uncomfortable position to say this is what you've been granted, we have not heard the amount of evidence we would have wished to hear and then make our -- draw our conclusions, make our determinations, and that's -- when I'm very insistent it is because the Chamber wants to hear the Defence evidence and the Chamber is not here to see whether this week perhaps we could see one witness and perhaps after three weeks we could hear another one. We want to -- we want the Defence to do everything -- and I repeat everything it can to present their evidence within the schedule we have given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with that entirely. I would only like to say this, Your Honour: That if -- and perhaps I'm wrong in doing this -- if I detect the slightest suggestion there that the Defence has not used its full application, its full industry, and its full inventiveness and is not doing its best in very difficult circumstances to bring these witnesses, then that implication is rejected utterly, Your Honour. We are doing our best in very difficult circumstances, we are reporting conscientiously to the Court and to the Prosecution appropriately at every moment, as appropriate, and we are doing our best. One of the witnesses that we were certainly hoping to bring is the witness Mr. Lakic, where we received the report about the death in his family. We received that report. What can we do except act on that, Your Honour? Mr. Lakic, if the Trial Chamber had not altered the timetable against the Defence's wishes, then Mr. Lakic might have given his evidence and be gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, ten lines ago, you said, "If I detect ..." There is no reason to detect any such thing and therefore in the ten following lines are totally superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm delighted to hear that, Your Honour, and I apologise if I misread anything or misheard anything that Your Honour has said in an overly sensitive way. Thank you for that confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not at all. I'm delighted to hear that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask for a little bit more time in relation to the D14 matter that was referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness could be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is en route to the courtroom, we earlier discussed an exhibit. It was tab 14. There was an issue as to the date of the -- handwritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- it said February 1992. I have a copy of the cover of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you show it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I showed it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you agree it was published when?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm prepared to make that agreement. If the Court would rather the document didn't go into the evidence, I'm neutral either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties agree, the Chamber is pleased to accept that, and it again underlines that the date on the bottom of an article is not necessarily the date of publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is Your Honour accepting the stipulation or does the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We accept that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So stipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's accepted it was a publication of February 1992. Mr. Harmon, you know that your time is very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I intend to put one document to the witness just to verify a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if you could turn to tab 32, please. This exhibit is already in evidence, P743. Mr. Poplasen, this is a document, it has a signature at the bottom. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document where you suggest to the Serb Municipality of Vogosca War Presidency, and in subpart 3, that the illegal prison in Vogosca be transformed into a subdivision of the correctional facilities in Butnim or Pale and that an investigative judge and warden be appointed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's under 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. I just wanted to verify this document with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you were asked about the use of the word "vojvoda" - excuse my pronunciation. I want to show you some documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I don't know how much time we are going to spend to that but the Chamber, on the basis of a lot of evidence, gained the impression that a vojvoda is not -- perhaps historically he was but at present not a kind of a military leader but someone with I would say moral authority, a kind of a moral leading person in society. That's our provisional impression of what a vojvoda is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can cut the matter short: We also have the definition of an archduke from an English dictionary, and it uses the same word, I can say. I can provide that but -- perhaps the witness could have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is an interview, Mr. Poplasen, with you in 1998 in a publication called Dani, and it's right, isn't it, that you are asked here about the use of the word "vojvoda" and you define it in the answer. If you quickly cast your eye over the B/C/S version - I'm not going to ask to you read it into the record - I'm going to ask you to confirm that you said this.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the text present -- which actually presents the viewpoint presented by His Honour, that it was a honourary and symbolic role which had nothing to do with military command. If need be, I can read the entire text, but that's -- these are the lines along which the text runs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Mr. Josse, I have a question which sounds perhaps a bit familiar to you, whether then only the translated portion or whether the original and the context would be in evidence? I noticed that it seems that in B/C/S, that the interview also is about extradition and about the Tribunal, et cetera. I don't know whether you wanted that to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't particularly. It would mean sending it for translation. I would rather leave it as it is for logistical as much as any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
