utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, no objection against that, limited to this? Of course, Mr. Harmon has the opportunity to ask for the context to be translated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, at this point I can't read it, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I see a few words which sound very familiar to me, Tribunal and extradition, so therefore -- but we know already something about the attitude of this witness towards the -- this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will look at the document at my first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for the time being it's given a number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D142, and it's limited to the translation -- translated portion, unless Mr. Harmon comes back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The learned Judge -- put that down, if you would, Mr. Poplasen. The learned Judge has just asked you about your views of the Tribunal. It's right, isn't it, that you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, I think in the year 2002.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor but not in relation to the Krajisnik case but in relation to the Seselj case, on the request of the OTP. The statement I gave which had to do with the Krajisnik case was given by me to Mr. Krajisnik's defence team, whereas it was in the Seselj case that I gave a statement to the members of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To be clear, was that a voluntary statement or were you forced in some way to make it, under some sort of compulsion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to interpret your word "voluntary." The entire NATO pact is behind all that. We were sitting at a desk, having coffee, and I was telling them the truth, the whole truth, just as I was doing right now, in my firm belief that I was the last person who would mind having the truth out. I even told them that, if need be, I can come and testify before the Tribunal. Now you're pushing me to say whether it's voluntary or not. Well, nobody actually does it voluntarily except for the people who work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was being a bit clumsy. It's right that you weren't a suspect, you weren't interviewed under caution, this is a statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was not cautioned. I was asked, requested, by the Prosecution to give a statement. There were no cautions leveled at me, that I was a possible suspect of any act, either by the OTP or by the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Next I want, if you would, to have a look at tab 8A. This is an interview. Quite large parts have been alluded to. I'm going to need the help of the usher here to find the part in B/C/S. But in the course of this interview, which we see took place in February 2000, you may take this from me, you were asked, "Does it bother you that non-Serbs are returning to RS?" And your answer was, "Why would it bother me? That is their personal business and a matter of their assessment where they want to live and organise their lives and their future." Do you remember giving that answer, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is indeed my opinion, and that is the answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next matter I'd like to turn to, please, relates to questions of paramilitaries that you were asked about at some length. I want to hand out another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, only a portion of this has been translated. I suspect the Chamber would want it all translated in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same -- yes, for such short documents the Chamber would like to have the context available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This in effect is a public announcement by you on behalf of your newly formed political party, dealing with the outline of its policies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see at number 3 on the first page what you had to say about paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. By your leave, I can read the paragraph. It's just one sentence. I believe the interpreters can successfully interpret it. If there is no English version, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. There is an English translation of that part, Mr. Poplasen. For that part, we have an English translation, so for my part you don't need to read it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, it bears noting that this release is from November of 1992. And it clearly shows that we do not organise or support the organising of other military formations and that we even want to rid ourselves of the negative heritage of the JNA, primarily of the communist type of conduct and ideology among the manpower. When you look at the press release as a whole, not just this point, then you can see that under point 4, for instance, we are insisting on the principle of legality and we insist that change in society cannot be brought about forcibly, but in a legal, lawful way. This is our viewpoint from 1992, which was for the most part the subject of our discussions in that period of time. It was published, or rather, broadcast by TV and published in the press. It was -- a part of it was even republished in one of my books.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite the Court to read in full tab 47, which I don't think there is a B/C/S version of. It was the extract from the video, the top of the second page in English I would draw the Court's attention to. I'm not going to ask the witness, simply through lack of time. I've got one other matter I wish to deal with before I sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd like us to read in full tab 47?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In due course, and in particular the top of the second page, the answer given by this witness in that interview at the top of the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Poplasen, you -- while this is being handed out, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check 47 has a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 47 does have a number but what doesn't have a number is the pamphlet which I handed out a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I hand out one other document, which will also need a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This -- you were telling the Court earlier about the double pension situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right that this is an extract from a newspaper. What's the name of the newspaper, please, to avoid me embarrassing myself by not being able to pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is the daily paper issued in the federation, in Sarajevo, called Nevniavas [phoen], as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. That's what it says on the page that we see. And it's right, again, Your Honour, we will have the whole of this translated, but basically there is a question from a reader about pension rights, and the answer is given that pursuant to Article 94 of the law of pensions - I'm summarising - that for persons who have taken part in BiH defence preparations or its defence between April the 30th 1991, December the 21st 1995, time so spent shall be counted double for persons in their retirement pensions. That's what it says, doesn't it, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite evidently this stems from this piece of legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, we will submit the whole of the question and answer to the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then receive -- of course, the Chamber would most -- would be most interested not only in how legislation is presented in the press but to have the original source available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am told we've got it, and I think that's the information that is about to be relayed to me. I'm told we have been sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the actual law, that someone can have the pleasure of translating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this would be federal legislation. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're asking the wrong man, plain and simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Is this federal legislation or is this -- how do I have to understand it? Perhaps we'd better look at it on the basis of the original text so that we can then identify to what extent this law would apply in any entity, and if it does apply only in one entity, whether similar legislation exists in the other entity which, of course, would give a more balanced view on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. At least we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Apparently that hasn't got a number. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D144, Your Honours, the extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I got a bit lost where it concerns D143, which was the pamphlet. Is that correct, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But exactly what pamphlet would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The public announcement by Nikola Poplasen on behalf of the newly formed political party dealing with the outline of its policies, dated 12 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me, yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one final question for you: Talking about detention and detention facilities in Vogosca and getting them under the -- under the system, could you tell us how many there were and whether this prison warden you talked about was in charge of them all, if there were more?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. Had I known of the existence of some other facility, I would have reacted accordingly. I really am not familiar with this. I'm not claiming that there wasn't any, I'm just saying that I wasn't aware of the existence of any other facility other than this one that I visited just for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it was not entirely clear how it came that you would visit that facility, because I think you said that you were having a cup of coffee there and you saw people move around. What made you go there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may seem unusual but it was a pure coincidence. With me in the vehicle was my friend, a commissioner from the adjacent municipality. He came up with this idea to have coffee at his acquaintance's, Brano Vlaco. I didn't know the man. And I asked him where the man was, and he told me he was over there -- that he was there, along the road, because it was a catering establishment, an inn of a sort. And then we simply strayed from the road and parked there and that was when I happened to see the facility. It was a coincidence. Then I asked him what this was all about and what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw as what you now say was a detention facility. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no armed guard in front of the building, but there, next to the bar, there were some people who seemed to be detainees but there were also people who did not seem to be detainees and they were wearing -- they had weapons slung over their arms. To the right there was a restaurant there. We sat at a table. Vlaco came and joined us and we engaged in a conversation. That was when I collected the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, if I come into a bar and see some people with perhaps rifles, and others not having any rifles, how would you see that those who have no weapons are detainees? In a bar, I would expect them to be visitors of a bar. What made you think of them as detainees?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the conversation with Mr. Vlaco, as I just mentioned. He told me what this was about, but it was quite confusing. I wasn't really clear whether this was a detention facility, whether this was a collection centre or a reception centre, and I asked him to clear this up because we could not leave the situation standing as it was, since it was obvious that one could leave the facility undisturbed. Nobody was there under duress. My conclusion was that perhaps the Muslims felt safer in this facility rather than somewhere else. Perhaps some of them there had had their houses -- had lost their houses, which had been burnt or something of the sort. It seemed even to me to have a character of a private prison, somebody thought of the idea of having a place where to detain people and then went and found some people and detained them, because there were such instances, and it is true the entire impression was as you mentioned, because you could see people passing by, some of them armed, some of them unarmed. That was the impression I was an able to gain in the 15 minutes I was there, and then on the basis of the conversation I had, I decided that I ought to react, which I did with the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that they were moving around, the detainees, so you gave us, by your language, the impression that they were, well, to some extent free, to some extent not. Could you explain that a bit more in detail. Did you see anyone move out and leave the street alone or --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 minutes isn't much. There was always someone entering and someone leaving the building. I can't say whether it was a soldier or whether it was someone come to visit someone else. There was nothing on the basis of which I could draw any such conclusion. On the basis of there having been movement there, I told you that I didn't feel that anybody was being closed, but when Vlaco told me that he had nothing to feed the people he held therewith, I realised that these people were in fact staying there and were not free in a way. Because Vlaco inviting us for lunch and then I asked him whether there was some food to be had there, because I could see some plates being taken from one place to another. He suggested a restaurant, then I complained about it and then we started discussing these matters, and as we discussed these matters, I was inferring what this was all about. It was all as we were talking that these -- these conclusions of mine were emerging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us that you got the impression that, as you said, you didn't feel that anybody was being closed, but do I understand then from the information you received from Vlaco, that they were actually detained?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is "to a certain extent" being detained? Were they free to leave the building and go to wherever they wanted to go or were they not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that they were. At a certain point Vlaco said that he had to secure food supplies for them, which meant that they were there every day. Now, these people who were there every day, whether they were able to leave or not, I could not tell. I didn't know. I thought it was a facility of a semi-open or an open type, so I suppose that some of them were in fact free to leave. There was, just around this time, a situation in front of the building where there was shooting going on, some such activity, and I thought that perhaps it was even safer to be in the building rather than outside of it, but my general impression was that something illegal was going on there. That's why I decided to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you then verify before you addressed the central organs about this? Because you're creating a picture which is quite confusing. People coming every day to fetch their food, free to leave perhaps or perhaps not, being detained but perhaps not being detained. I take it that you -- you had a feeling in the beginning that there was some -- well, that people were free to move but then you were told that they were not and then -- what did you actually write in, as you said, to the government, that this detention facility should be under the -- under the normal prison system?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I'm not creating a picture that is confusing. It's rather the circumstances and the situation itself that was quite confusing. And I was confused. I was puzzled. When I went over to the municipality, I asked them about the facility and they provided me with a puzzling answer and I realised that none of the authorities had a clear picture of the situation. Then I told them that such a situation could not be tolerated, that people could not be allowed to do things at their own will, that something had to be done about it, which resulted in my reaction in writing. My conclusion is that the authorities knew about it before, and I did not in fact ask the local authorities to do something about it but I addressed the republican authorities. My opinion was that had the local authorities wanted to do something about it, they would have done it -- they would have done it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ask about the existence of similar facilities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked them whether there was any other and the answer was no. Nobody informed me of any other such facilities and I didn't really know of the existence of any. Had I known, I would have reacted in a similar or even harsher way, depending on what I would find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Does this raise any -- I have to apologise for -- I'm looking now at the clock, I see that we are far beyond our time. I apologise, but Mr. Harmon, would you take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I certainly will, Your Honour, I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could look at the monitor, we'll see -- Your Honours will see a photograph which was displayed to the witness yesterday in his -- it is P379. It is a photograph of Planjo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Poplasen, if you could turn to tab 31, which needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 31, Your Honours, will be P1097.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you were appointed as the War Commissioner for Vogosca on the 18th of June. This document is a document from the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, Municipal Secretariat for Town Planning, Property Rights, Relations, Housing Policy and Land Register. It's dated the 8th of July, which is approximately three weeks after you were appointed, and it is a decision based on the war staff, a decision of the 7th of July, of then the Municipal Secretariat for Town Planning made a decision, which I will read into the record: "1. The house of Planjo Almas and Miralem Semizovac is given for use to the Ministry of Justice for the needs of the prison of Serbian Municipality of Vogosca. "This decision is of a temporary character, and will be valid until the end of the war conflict; i.e., until there is a need and until there is no legal action in the sense of acquiring the ownership over aforesaid mentioned real estate." So the explanation: "Based on the request of the Ministry of Justice, the Department of Butmir Prison of Serbian Municipality of Vogosca and a decision of the war staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vogosca issued at the session of the 7th of July 1992, Municipal Secretariat for Town Planning, Property Rights Relations, Housing Policy and Land Register - issued this decision." And it's signed by Secretary Predrag Bejatovic. Now, did you know Mr. Predrag Bejatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How does this arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It arises directly out of the question that was asked by Judge Orie if there were other prisons in the municipality of Vogosca and whether this witness was aware of them. So this document is relevant because this witness was a war commissioner for three weeks by the time this decision was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that you are withdrawing your objection, so please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Poplasen, do you know Predrag Bejatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document, and I hear of this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp is probably that of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. All the municipalities had the same stamps but, of course, different titles and this bearing this coat of arms with four Cs in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document says, Mr. Poplasen, that there was in fact a prison in Poplasa [phoen] at the house of Planjo and that it existed for approximately three weeks after you were named as a war commissioner. Is it your evidence before this Court that the only prison facility in the municipality of Vogosca that you were aware of was the residence at -- or at Sonja's place and that you were completely unaware of this prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither this nor any other -- or rather, neither of the options. I didn't know of the prisons and I'm not familiar with this document either, what I can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- it's translated at the, under 1, in this document -- no, not under 1. The heading, it says: "Based on the decision of the war staff ..." What's the war staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation], I don't know, I'm not familiar with that. I'm not familiar with the wording, document, its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which war staff? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can't enlighten us in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I make it clear, Your Honour: I cut my re-examination short, I would have re-examined on tab 32, would have asked about various other things on this issue. Cut it short. Your Honour asked a lot of questions. I don't take exception to that. I do take some exception to my learned friend's questions thereafter. Basically, it was the second bite of the cherry. That's what it amounted to really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any, then, specific questions you would like to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the interpreters because I'm the one who is mainly responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to be a moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's Friday, of course, we would like to finish the witness today. Further examination by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 32, Mr. Poplasen, which you were shown at the end of the first batch of cross-examination by my learned friend. Is this the report that you were telling the Court about? The report to the republican authorities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the reports. There must be another one somewhere, one of the minutes that was sent to Koljevic. The request sent to the government had to do with the prison only and is more extensive. In the heading it should say the republican government, Justice Ministry. I believe that what you have just shown me here is my first report that I drafted the day after my visit to the municipality, which I sent to Mr. Koljevic. I sent the request to the government later on. I don't know whether it was a day or two or later the same day. Why this request is nowhere to be seen, I don't know, but it was properly delivered to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I may take it from your last answer, Mr. Poplasen, where you said you sent it to Mr. Koljevic, at least the report was addressed to the Wartime Presidency. You would agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the position. I don't know if I need to give any additional comments. It was sent to Mr. Koljevic. I don't think Mr. Koljevic forwarded it to the government because I subsequently wrote to the government about this prison matter. I wanted the Presidency to have an insight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There is no suggestion that Mr. Koljevic would have sent it to the government but, of course, there was a possible implication that it was addressed to the Wartime Presidency, and that's what you just confirmed, that you wanted the Presidency to know about the situation. This was my last question. If there are no further questions, Mr. Poplasen, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer to all questions put to you by both parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Poplasen out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one brief message I'd leave to the parties. A request has been made to start with the next witness on Tuesday rather than on Monday. The parties will be informed about it this afternoon, whether this suggestion will be followed by the Chamber, yes or no, through the usual channels of communication, but the parties should be prepared, at least as it stands now, to start on Monday. We will then -- with, of course, this reservation, we will adjourn until next Monday, quarter past two, same courtroom.
